core.p: Many marks are lost on units. The total area and the quadrat area **must be in the same units** before you divide.
bullets: Area of a square or rectangle = length x width
A 50 cm x 50 cm quadrat = 2500 cm2 = 0.25 m2
**1 hectare (ha) = 10 000 m2** (an area of 100 m x 100 m)
Convert to m2 first, then divide

callouts.p: Write the conversion as a line of working, e.g. 2.5 ha = 2.5 x 10 000 = 25 000 m2. Even if the final answer is wrong you can pick up method marks.

core.p: When individuals cannot be counted, the raw data is **percentage cover**. You can average the cover from many quadrats and use it to estimate the **area** of the habitat covered by that species.
bullets: In a grid quadrat, % cover = number of squares more than half covered x % per square
25-square grid: each square = 4%; 100-square grid: each square = 1%
Mean % cover = total of % covers / number of quadrats
Area covered = mean % cover / 100 x total area
Example: mean cover 30% on a 200 m2 lawn = 0.30 x 200 = **60 m2** covered
Total cover in a quadrat can add up to more than 100% if plants grow in layers over each other

core.p: **Frequency** tells you how often a species turns up in your samples. It is quick to measure because you only record whether the species is present or absent in each quadrat.
bullets: Frequency (%) = number of quadrats containing the species / total number of quadrats x 100
Example: daisies found in 14 of 20 quadrats = 14 / 20 x 100 = **70%**
Frequency does not tell you how many individuals there are
A species can have high frequency but low abundance (a few plants spread everywhere), or the reverse (lots of plants in one clump)

core.p: With a belt transect, the aim is not one population total but **how abundance changes with distance** or with an abiotic factor. You process the data at each point along the line.
bullets: If the transect was repeated, calculate the **mean count at each distance**
Plot **distance** on the x-axis and mean number or % cover on the y-axis
Plot the abiotic factor (e.g. light intensity) on the same graph or a second axis
Describe the trend using **numbers from the data**, e.g. 'rises from 2 at 0 m to 18 at 10 m'
Look for a **correlation** between the species and the abiotic factor
Explain the trend using biology, e.g. more light means more photosynthesis, so more growth
Remember that **correlation is not causation**: other factors also change along the transect

callouts.p: In 'describe the pattern' questions, one mark is often for quoting two values with units from the table or graph.

core.p: The more samples you take, the closer your mean is likely to be to the true mean of the whole area. Anomalous results can distort the mean and should be spotted.
bullets: An **anomaly** is a result that does not fit the pattern of the rest of the data
Check anomalies for an obvious cause, such as a quadrat placed on a path or a counting mistake
If you exclude an anomaly, **divide by the reduced number** of quadrats
Taking **more quadrats** reduces the effect of any single unusual one
Organisms that are **clumped** need more quadrats than evenly spread ones
Repeating the sampling and getting similar means shows the results are **repeatable**

core.p: Every population estimate depends on assumptions. Grade 9 answers explain why the estimate might be too high or too low.
bullets: Assumes the quadrats are **representative** of the whole area
Assumes organisms are spread fairly **evenly**; if clumped, a few random quadrats may miss or hit clumps
Assumes species were **identified correctly** and counted consistently
Animals that move (e.g. snails) may leave or enter quadrats during counting, so quadrats work best for **plants and slow-moving organisms**
A small number of quadrats gives a less reliable estimate
Improve the estimate by **increasing the number of random quadrats** and using a clear counting rule

callouts.p: Never write that the method gives the exact population. Say it gives an estimate, and explain what could make it inaccurate.

analogy.t: Counting sweets in a giant jar
analogy.p: Imagine guessing how many sweets are in a huge jar. You scoop out a few cupfuls, count the sweets in each, find the mean per cup, then work out how many cups would fit in the jar and multiply. Each cupful is a quadrat, the jar is the field, and 'how many cups fit' is total area / quadrat area. The analogy breaks down because sweets can be mixed so they are evenly spread, whereas plants in a field are often clumped in some places and missing in others, which is why random placing and many quadrats are so important.

terms.d: All the organisms of one species living in a particular area at the same time.
An approximate value worked out from samples rather than counting every individual.
A square frame of known area used to take a sample of organisms.
The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when data are arranged in order.
The value that occurs most often in a data set.
The difference between the highest and lowest values.
The number of individuals of a species per unit area, such as per m2.
The proportion of a quadrat's area covered by a species, expressed as a percentage.
The percentage of quadrats in which a species is present.
The number of individuals of a species, or the amount of area it covers, in a habitat.
A unit of area equal to 10 000 m2.
A result that does not fit the pattern shown by the rest of the data.
A sample that accurately reflects the whole area being studied.
A line of quadrats placed at regular intervals across a habitat to show how organisms change along it.

mistakes.w: A 0.5 m x 0.5 m quadrat has an area of 0.5 m2.
Population = mean per quadrat x total area.
mistakes.r: Population = mean per quadrat x (total area / area of one quadrat); this only equals mean x area when the quadrat is 1 m2.

mistakes.w: Dividing the total count by only the quadrats that contained organisms.
mistakes.r: Divide by the total number of quadrats, including those with zero.

mistakes.w: Mixing units, e.g. dividing an area in m2 by a quadrat area in cm2.
mistakes.r: Convert both areas to the same unit (usually m2) before dividing.

mistakes.w: 1 hectare = 1000 m2.
mistakes.r: 1 hectare = 10 000 m2.

mistakes.w: The method tells you exactly how many plants there are.
mistakes.r: It gives an estimate, which assumes the samples are representative.

mistakes.w: Take more quadrats to make it more accurate.
mistakes.r: Take more random quadrats so the mean is more representative / reduces the effect of anomalies.

mistakes.w: Describing a transect graph without using numbers.
mistakes.r: Quote values from the data with units to describe the trend.

exam.q: Calculate the area of a quadrat that measures 0.5 m by 0.5 m.
exam.tip: Multiply the sides; do not just halve.

exam.q: State the equation used to estimate population size from quadrat data.
model: Population = mean number per quadrat x (total area / area of one quadrat)
exam.tip: Learn it in words.

exam.q: A student counted 3, 5, 0, 4, 6, 2, 7, 5, 4, 4 dandelions in 10 quadrats. Calculate the mean number per quadrat.
model: Total = 40
Mean = 40 / 10 = 4 dandelions per quadrat
exam.tip: Include the zero and divide by 10.

exam.q: Using the data above, give the median and the range.
model: Median = 4 (ordered: 0,2,3,4,4,4,5,5,6,7; middle two are 4 and 4)
Range = 7 - 0 = 7
exam.tip: Order first.

exam.q: A field measures 80 m by 50 m. The mean number of buttercups in a 0.25 m2 quadrat is 3. Estimate the number of buttercups in the field.
model: Field area = 80 x 50 = 4000 m2
3 x 16 000 = 48 000 buttercups
exam.tip: Show each step for method marks.

exam.q: A 1 m2 quadrat was used in a 2 hectare meadow. The mean number of orchids was 0.4 per quadrat. Estimate the orchid population.
exam.tip: Convert hectares to m2 first.

exam.q: Clover was present in 18 of 24 quadrats. Calculate the frequency of clover.
exam.tip: Frequency is about presence, not numbers.

exam.q: The mean percentage cover of moss on a 150 m2 lawn was 20%. Calculate the area of lawn covered by moss.
exam.tip: Convert the percentage to a decimal first.

exam.q: Explain why the student's population estimate may not be accurate, and suggest how to improve it.
model: Only a small number of quadrats used / small sample
Plants may be clumped / unevenly distributed
So sample may not be representative of the whole field
Improve by using more quadrats placed at random coordinates
exam.tip: Give reasons, then a matching improvement.

exam.q: Explain how a student could use quadrats to estimate the population of daisies on a school field, including the calculation they would carry out.
model: Measure the length and width of the field and calculate total area
Use two tape measures and random number generator to choose coordinates
Place a quadrat (e.g. 0.25 m2) at each coordinate
Count daisies in each quadrat; use at least 10 quadrats
Calculate mean number per quadrat (total / number of quadrats)
Population = mean x (total area / quadrat area)
State that the result is an estimate
exam.tip: Combine the method and the maths in one logical sequence.

worked.q: A student placed 12 random 0.5 m x 0.5 m quadrats in a 1.5 hectare meadow and counted a total of 84 cowslips. Estimate the cowslip population.
steps: Mean per quadrat = 84 / 12 = 7
Quadrat area = 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 m2
Meadow area = 1.5 x 10 000 = 15 000 m2
Number of quadrats that fit = 15 000 / 0.25 = 60 000
Population = 7 x 60 000 = 420 000
worked.ans: Estimated population = 420 000 cowslips (an estimate, because it assumes the 12 quadrats are representative).

worked.q: Counts in 8 quadrats were 5, 6, 4, 5, 31, 6, 5, 4. Identify the anomaly and calculate the mean with and without it.
steps: 31 is far higher than all other values (4 to 6), so it is the anomaly
Mean with anomaly = 66 / 8 = 8.25
Mean without anomaly = 35 / 7 = 5.0
The anomaly raised the mean by over 3 plants per quadrat, which would greatly overestimate the population
Check the quadrat for a reason, e.g. it landed on a dense clump
worked.ans: The anomaly is 31; the mean is 8.25 with it and 5.0 without it (dividing by 7).

worked.q: A belt transect was repeated 3 times. At 4 m from a hedge the counts were 9, 12 and 15. At 8 m the counts were 18, 21 and 24. Calculate the mean at each distance and describe the trend.
steps: Trend: the mean number of plants increases from 12 at 4 m to 21 at 8 m as distance from the hedge increases
worked.ans: Mean = 12 at 4 m and 21 at 8 m, so abundance increases with distance from the hedge.

bio_edx.8.10.summary: Carbon is the key element in every organic molecule (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and DNA), so it must be recycled for life to continue. In the **carbon cycle**, **photosynthesis** removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, **feeding** passes carbon along food chains, and **respiration**, **combustion** and **decomposition** return it to the air. **Microorganisms** (bacteria and fungi) act as **decomposers**: they secrete enzymes to digest dead organisms and waste, and their respiration releases the carbon as CO2, while conditions that stop decay lead to carbon being locked up as **fossil fuels**.

core.h: Why the carbon cycle is important
core.p: Every living cell is built from carbon compounds. The amount of carbon on Earth is fixed, so the carbon in dead organisms and waste must be returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, ready for plants to use in photosynthesis again.
bullets: Carbon is found in **all organic molecules**: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids (DNA).
Plants need a constant supply of **CO2 for photosynthesis**; without recycling, atmospheric CO2 would run out and food chains would collapse.
The cycle keeps the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere **roughly balanced**, because processes that remove CO2 are matched by processes that release it.
CO2 is a **greenhouse gas**, so the balance of the carbon cycle affects global temperature.
Human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation are upsetting this balance.

callouts.p: The carbon cycle returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis.

fig.cap: The carbon cycle. Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air; respiration by plants, animals and decomposers, and combustion of fossil fuels, return it. Slow decay over millions of years forms fossil fuels.

core.p: Carbon is held in several **stores**. It moves between them by the processes of the cycle. Some stores exchange carbon quickly; others lock it away for millions of years.
bullets: **Atmosphere**: carbon dioxide gas (about 0.04% of air).
**Living organisms**: carbon in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and DNA of plants, animals and microorganisms.
**Dead organic matter**: leaf litter, dead bodies, faeces and soil humus.
**Oceans**: CO2 dissolves in sea water; marine organisms use it to make shells of calcium carbonate.
**Fossil fuels**: coal, oil and natural gas formed from organisms that did not fully decay.
**Rocks**: limestone and chalk formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms.

core.h: Photosynthesis: removing carbon from the air
core.p: Photosynthesis is the only major process that takes carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and turns it into organic compounds. It is carried out by **producers**: green plants and algae (including phytoplankton in the oceans).
bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen (using light energy, in chloroplasts).
Carbon from CO2 becomes part of **glucose**.
Glucose is converted into **starch** (storage), **cellulose** (cell walls), **lipids**, and, with nitrate ions, **amino acids and proteins**.
So carbon from the air ends up in the **biomass** of the plant.
Algae and phytoplankton in the oceans carry out a large share of global photosynthesis.

callouts.p: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air. Do not say plants release CO2 by photosynthesis; they release CO2 by respiration.

core.h: Feeding: passing carbon along food chains
core.p: When animals eat plants or other animals, the carbon compounds in the food are **digested** and **absorbed**, then used to build the animal's own tissues or used in respiration.
bullets: Primary consumers get carbon by eating producers; secondary consumers get it by eating primary consumers.
Large molecules (starch, protein, fat) are digested into small soluble molecules (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol).
These are absorbed into the blood and built into the animal's own **carbohydrates, proteins and lipids**.
Not all carbon eaten becomes new biomass: much is released by respiration and some is lost in **faeces**.
This is why biomass decreases at each trophic level.

core.h: Respiration: returning carbon to the air
core.p: All living organisms, including **plants, animals and microorganisms**, respire all the time. Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose to release energy and produces carbon dioxide, which diffuses into the atmosphere.
bullets: Word equation: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (energy released).
Plants respire **24 hours a day**; in daylight, photosynthesis is usually faster, so there is a net uptake of CO2.
Animals release CO2 from respiration when they breathe out.
Decomposers release CO2 from respiration as they feed on dead matter.
Respiration is therefore the main way carbon returns from the biotic to the abiotic part of the cycle.

callouts.p: Plants photosynthesise (in light only) and respire (all the time). Only photosynthesis removes CO2.

core.h: The role of microorganisms as decomposers
core.p: When plants and animals die, or produce waste such as faeces, urine and fallen leaves, their carbon is locked in organic molecules. **Decomposers**, mainly **bacteria and fungi**, release this carbon back to the atmosphere.
bullets: Decomposers **secrete enzymes** onto dead material; this is **extracellular digestion**.
Enzymes such as carbohydrases, proteases and lipases break **large insoluble molecules** into **small soluble molecules** such as sugars and amino acids.
Decomposers **absorb** these small molecules into their cells.
They use them in **respiration**, releasing **carbon dioxide** into the atmosphere (and soil air).
Some carbon becomes part of the decomposers' own biomass, which is later broken down when they die.
Decomposition also releases **mineral ions** into the soil for plants to absorb.
**Detritivores** such as earthworms, woodlice and maggots break dead matter into small pieces, increasing the **surface area** for microorganisms.

callouts.p: Microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide by respiration and mineral ions into the soil.
Decomposers do not release CO2 by digesting; the CO2 comes from their respiration of the digested products.

core.p: Decomposers are living organisms using enzymes, so the rate of decay depends on conditions that affect their growth and enzyme activity. This explains why carbon is recycled quickly in some places and stored in others.
bullets: **Warm temperatures** increase enzyme activity and microorganism reproduction, so decay is faster (up to an optimum; very high temperatures denature enzymes).
**Moisture** is needed for microorganisms to grow and for enzymes to work.
**Oxygen** is needed for aerobic respiration by most decomposers, so decay is faster in well-aerated conditions.
A larger **surface area** of dead material (e.g. chopped by detritivores) speeds up decay.
Cold, dry, acidic or **waterlogged** (anaerobic) conditions slow or stop decay, so carbon stays locked in dead material.

callouts.p: 9.17B to 9.19B go further into how temperature, water and oxygen affect decay in food preservation and composting.

core.p: If dead organisms are buried in conditions where decomposers cannot work, such as waterlogged, anaerobic or acidic mud, the carbon is not released. Over **millions of years**, heat and pressure turn this material into **fossil fuels**.
bullets: **Coal** formed from plants in ancient swamps that did not fully decay.
**Oil and natural gas** formed from tiny marine organisms (plankton) buried in sediment.
**Peat** forms today in cold, waterlogged, acidic bogs where decay is very slow.
Carbon in fossil fuels is removed from the fast cycle for millions of years.
Shells and skeletons of marine organisms (calcium carbonate) can form **limestone**, another long-term carbon store.

core.p: **Combustion** (burning) of fossil fuels and of wood or other biomass releases the carbon in them as carbon dioxide. Burning fossil fuels returns carbon to the atmosphere that had been locked away for millions of years.
bullets: Word equation (for a hydrocarbon fuel): fuel + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
Combustion of fossil fuels for electricity, transport and industry adds CO2 much faster than photosynthesis can remove it.
Burning forests to clear land releases CO2 and also removes trees that would have absorbed CO2.
This is a major reason why atmospheric CO2 concentration has been rising since the Industrial Revolution.

core.p: Before large-scale human activity, the processes removing CO2 from the air (mainly photosynthesis) and those adding it (respiration and decomposition) were roughly balanced. Human activity has tipped this balance.
bullets: Removes CO2: **photosynthesis** by plants and algae; CO2 dissolving in oceans.
Adds CO2: **respiration** by all organisms (including decomposers), **combustion**.
**Deforestation** reduces photosynthesis and, if trees are burned or left to rot, adds CO2.
**Burning fossil fuels** adds CO2 from long-term stores.
Increased CO2 enhances the greenhouse effect, contributing to **global warming** and climate change.
Reforestation and reducing fossil fuel use help restore the balance.

head: Removes CO2 from air
Adds CO2 to air
rows: Formation of fossil fuels and limestone (very slow)
Combustion of fossil fuels and wood

callouts.p: Photosynthesis is the main process removing CO2; several processes add it.

fig.cap: The carbon balance: processes that remove CO2 from the atmosphere on the left, processes that add it on the right. Burning fossil fuels and deforestation tip the balance so atmospheric CO2 rises.

core.p: Edexcel questions often show a carbon cycle diagram with missing processes, or ask you to explain how carbon in one organism ends up in another or in the air.
bullets: Name each process precisely: **photosynthesis, respiration, feeding / consumption, death, decomposition, combustion, fossilisation**.
State the form of carbon at each step: CO2 in air, glucose / carbohydrates in plants, proteins and fats in animals.
Always mention that decomposers are **microorganisms (bacteria and fungi)** that **respire** to release CO2.
Mention **enzymes** when describing decay.
For 6-mark questions, follow one carbon atom all the way round the cycle in order.

callouts.p: Learn a checklist: photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, death and decomposition, fossilisation, combustion.

analogy.p: Think of the atmosphere as a current account of carbon. Photosynthesis is a withdrawal: plants take carbon out to build their bodies. Respiration and decomposition are deposits: carbon is paid back in. Decomposers are the bank clerks who process the dead accounts, so the carbon tied up in dead organisms is returned rather than lost. Fossil fuels are a savings account locked for millions of years; combustion is like suddenly emptying those savings into the current account, so the balance rises faster than plants can withdraw it. The analogy breaks down because a bank creates and destroys money, whereas carbon atoms are never created or destroyed, and because real processes run at the same time everywhere rather than as separate transactions.

terms.d: The continuous movement of carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans and rocks by photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition, combustion and fossilisation.
The process in which producers use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
The process in all living cells that releases energy from glucose; aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead organisms and waste, releasing CO2 by respiration and mineral ions into the soil.
The breakdown of dead organic matter by decomposers using enzymes.
Digestion outside the cell: enzymes are secreted onto food and the soluble products are absorbed.
An animal such as an earthworm or woodlouse that feeds on dead material, breaking it into smaller pieces.
Burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water.
Coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from remains of organisms that did not fully decay.
The slow formation of fossils or fossil fuels from buried remains under conditions where decay cannot happen.
A place where carbon is held, such as the atmosphere, organisms, oceans, fossil fuels or rocks.
The mass of living material in organisms, which contains stored carbon.
A gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that absorbs and re-emits heat, warming the Earth.
The large-scale removal of trees, which reduces photosynthesis and can release stored carbon.
A carbon-based molecule made by living organisms, such as glucose, protein, lipid or DNA.

mistakes.w: Plants give out carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.
mistakes.r: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and gives out oxygen; plants release CO2 by respiration.

mistakes.w: Plants respire only at night.
mistakes.r: Plants respire all the time; at night they only respire because photosynthesis needs light.

mistakes.w: Decomposers break down dead things and release carbon.
mistakes.r: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) secrete enzymes to digest dead matter and release carbon dioxide by respiration.

mistakes.w: Animals only return carbon when they die.
mistakes.r: Animals release CO2 continuously by respiration; decomposers release the rest after death.

mistakes.w: Fossil fuels are made when decomposers break down dead organisms.
mistakes.r: Fossil fuels form when decay is prevented (e.g. anaerobic, waterlogged, acidic conditions) so carbon is not released.

mistakes.w: Burning fossil fuels creates new carbon.
mistakes.r: Combustion releases carbon that had been locked in fossil fuels for millions of years; carbon is not created.

mistakes.w: Carbon moves from plants to animals by respiration.
mistakes.r: Carbon moves from plants to animals by feeding / eating (consumption), then digestion and absorption.

mistakes.w: Decomposition happens fastest in cold, dry conditions to preserve food.
mistakes.r: Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist conditions with oxygen; cold and dry conditions slow it down.

exam.q: Name the process that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
model: Photosynthesis.
exam.tip: Only photosynthesis is a major remover.

exam.q: Name two types of microorganism that act as decomposers.
model: Bacteria.
Fungi.
exam.tip: Viruses are not decomposers.

exam.q: State two processes that release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
model: Any two: respiration; combustion; decomposition / respiration of decomposers.
exam.tip: Be specific: respiration, not breathing.

exam.q: Explain how carbon in a dead leaf is returned to the atmosphere.
model: Decomposers / bacteria and fungi feed on the leaf.
They secrete enzymes that digest / break down the organic molecules.
They respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the air.
exam.tip: Enzymes plus respiration gets full marks.

exam.q: Explain the importance of the carbon cycle for living organisms.
model: Carbon is needed to make organic molecules / all living organisms contain carbon.
Recycling returns CO2 to the air so plants can photosynthesise / carbon is finite.
exam.tip: Link to photosynthesis needing CO2.

exam.q: Describe how carbon in the atmosphere becomes part of a protein in a rabbit.
model: Plants absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
Carbon becomes part of glucose, which is converted into proteins / other organic molecules (using nitrates).
Rabbit eats the plant and digests proteins into amino acids.
Amino acids absorbed and used to build the rabbit's own proteins.
exam.tip: Include digestion and absorption for the last two marks.

exam.q: Explain why dead bodies in a waterlogged peat bog decay very slowly.
model: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen.
Decomposers need oxygen for aerobic respiration.
So fewer decomposers / slower respiration and enzyme activity / acidic and cold conditions also slow decay.
exam.tip: Link oxygen to decomposer respiration.

exam.q: Explain how deforestation increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
model: Fewer trees so less photosynthesis, so less CO2 removed.
Trees burned releasing CO2 by combustion.
Or trees left to decay, decomposers respire releasing CO2.
exam.tip: Give both the reduced removal and the increased release.

exam.q: Suggest why earthworms increase the rate at which carbon is recycled.
model: Earthworms break dead material into smaller pieces.
Increasing the surface area for decomposers / enzymes to act on.
exam.tip: Surface area is the key phrase.

exam.q: Explain how fossil fuels form and how they affect the carbon cycle when burned.
model: Organisms die in conditions where decomposers cannot work (anaerobic / waterlogged / acidic).
So carbon is not released and remains buried; over millions of years with heat and pressure they form coal, oil or gas.
Combustion releases this stored carbon as CO2.
Adding CO2 faster than photosynthesis can remove it, so atmospheric CO2 rises.
exam.tip: Explain why decay did not happen.

exam.q: Explain the importance of the carbon cycle, including the processes involved and the role of microorganisms.
model: Carbon is needed in all organic molecules and the amount is finite, so it must be recycled.
Photosynthesis by plants and algae removes CO2 from the atmosphere and converts it to glucose and other organic compounds.
Carbon passes along food chains by feeding; digestion and absorption build it into consumer tissues.
Respiration by plants and animals releases CO2 back into the atmosphere.
When organisms die or produce waste, microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) secrete enzymes to decompose them and respire, releasing CO2.
Combustion of fossil fuels and wood releases carbon; where decay is prevented, carbon is stored as fossil fuels.
exam.tip: Go round the whole cycle in order and give microorganisms a full sentence about enzymes and respiration.

worked.q: A tree takes in 50 kg of carbon per year by photosynthesis. It releases 20 kg by its own respiration, and 25 kg of carbon in its fallen leaves is released by decomposers. How much carbon is stored in the tree's biomass each year, and what percentage of the carbon taken in is returned to the air?
steps: Carbon stored = 50 - 20 - 25 = 5 kg per year.
Carbon returned to air = 20 + 25 = 45 kg.
Percentage returned = 45 / 50 x 100 = 90%.
So only 10% of the carbon taken in is stored as new wood each year; most is recycled quickly.
worked.ans: 5 kg of carbon stored per year; 90% of carbon taken in is returned to the atmosphere.

worked.q: Model 4-mark answer: explain why the carbon dioxide concentration in a forest is lower at midday than at midnight.
steps: At midday there is light, so plants photosynthesise.
The rate of photosynthesis is greater than the rate of respiration, so there is a net uptake of CO2.
At midnight there is no light, so no photosynthesis takes place.
Plants, animals and decomposers continue to respire, releasing CO2, so its concentration rises.
worked.ans: Photosynthesis exceeds respiration in daylight, removing CO2; at night only respiration occurs, so CO2 builds up.

worked.q: An investigation measured CO2 released from leaf litter at 5 C and 25 C: 12 cm3 per hour and 48 cm3 per hour. Calculate how many times faster decay was at 25 C and explain the result.
steps: Decay (measured by CO2 release) was 4 times faster at 25 C.
At higher temperature decomposer enzymes have more kinetic energy, so more successful collisions with substrate molecules.
Microorganisms also grow and reproduce faster, so more respiration and more CO2 released.
worked.ans: 4 times faster at 25 C, because decomposer enzyme activity and microorganism growth increase with temperature (below the optimum).

bio_edx.8.11.summary: Water moves constantly between the sea, the air, living things and the land in the **water cycle**, driven by energy from the Sun. The key processes are **evaporation**, **transpiration**, **condensation** and **precipitation**, and together they deliver fresh water to land so that plants and animals can survive. In some dry countries there is not enough fresh water, so **potable water** (water safe to drink) is made from seawater by **desalination**, using either **distillation** or **reverse osmosis**.

core.p: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the oceans, the atmosphere, the land and living organisms. No new water is made: the same water is recycled over and over, changing state between liquid, gas (water vapour) and solid (ice and snow).
bullets: The cycle is **driven by heat energy from the Sun**, which makes water evaporate.
Water changes state: liquid to gas (evaporation), gas to liquid (condensation).
It links **abiotic** parts (sea, air, rocks, soil) with **biotic** parts (plants and animals).
It is one of the material cycles, like the carbon and nitrogen cycles, but no decomposers are needed to release the water.
Fresh water on land is constantly topped up by precipitation, even though most of Earth's water is salty sea water.

callouts.p: The continuous cycling of water between the oceans, the atmosphere, land and living organisms by evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation.

fig.cap: The water cycle. Heat from the Sun evaporates water from the sea and drives transpiration from plants. The water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation. Water returns to the sea by run-off and rivers.

core.p: Evaporation is when liquid water turns into water vapour. Heat energy from the Sun gives water molecules at the surface enough energy to escape into the air. Most evaporation happens from the surface of the sea, but water also evaporates from lakes, rivers, puddles and wet soil.
bullets: Energy source: **heat from the Sun**.
Faster when it is **warm**, **windy** and the air is **dry**.
When sea water evaporates, the **salt is left behind**, so the water vapour is fresh water.
This is why rain is fresh even though most of it started in the salty sea.
Warm water vapour rises because warm air is less dense.

callouts.p: Only water molecules leave the sea surface; dissolved salts stay behind. Evaporation is nature's distillation.

core.p: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants, mainly through the stomata. Water is taken up by the roots, travels up the xylem and evaporates from the surfaces of cells inside the leaf before diffusing out through the stomata.
bullets: Water enters roots from the soil, moves up the **xylem**, and leaves as vapour through **stomata**.
Transpiration returns huge amounts of water to the atmosphere, especially from forests.
It is faster in **warm, bright, windy, dry** conditions.
Removing forests (deforestation) reduces transpiration, so less water vapour forms clouds and there can be **less rainfall** in that area.
Both plants and animals also release some water vapour by **respiration** and animals by sweating and breathing out.

callouts.t: Transpiration is not evaporation from the sea
callouts.p: In the exam, only use transpiration for water vapour lost from plant leaves. Water leaving the sea or a lake is evaporation.

core.p: As warm, moist air rises it cools down. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapour, so the water vapour turns back into tiny liquid water droplets. This is condensation, and the droplets form clouds.
bullets: Condensation: **water vapour (gas) cools and turns into liquid water droplets**.
Air cools as it rises higher in the atmosphere, for example over mountains.
Billions of tiny droplets together make a **cloud**.
Clouds can be carried over land by the wind, which moves water from the sea to the land.
Condensation also gives dew on grass on cold mornings.

core.p: When the water droplets in clouds join together and become too heavy to stay in the air, they fall to the ground as precipitation. Precipitation includes rain, snow, sleet and hail.
bullets: Precipitation = water falling from clouds as **rain, snow, sleet or hail**.
It supplies **fresh water** to the land: rivers, lakes, soil and groundwater.
Some water soaks into the soil and rock (**infiltration**) and is stored as **groundwater** in aquifers.
Some water flows over the surface as **run-off** into streams and rivers and back to the sea.
Plants absorb soil water through their roots; animals drink it or get it from food.

head: Process
Change
Where it happens
rows: Cool air high in the atmosphere
Droplets fall as rain, snow or hail
From clouds to land and sea

core.h: Why the water cycle is important
core.p: Living organisms need water for almost every process of life, and the water cycle is how fresh water reaches the land. Without it, the land would dry out and terrestrial life could not survive.
bullets: Water is needed by plants for **photosynthesis** and to keep cells **turgid** for support.
Water transports substances: dissolved minerals in xylem, food in phloem, and substances in blood plasma.
Chemical reactions in cells take place in solution, so cells need water.
Water is lost all the time by transpiration, sweating, breathing and excretion, so it must be replaced.
The water cycle **cleans** water: evaporation leaves behind salts and many pollutants.
It provides **fresh water for humans** to drink, for farming (irrigation) and industry.

callouts.p: For importance questions, link the cycle to a use: provides fresh water on land, which plants need for photosynthesis and animals need to drink.

core.p: Potable water is water that is safe for humans to drink. It is not the same as pure water: it may still contain some dissolved substances, but the levels of salts, microorganisms and harmful chemicals are low enough to be safe.
bullets: Potable water has **low levels of dissolved salts** and **no harmful microorganisms**.
Pure water contains only water molecules; potable water does not have to be pure.
In the UK most potable water comes from rain that collects in reservoirs, lakes, rivers and aquifers.
This fresh water is treated by filtering and sterilising (for example with chlorine) before use.
Sea water is **not potable**: it has far too much salt.

callouts.p: Water that is safe to drink.

core.h: Why drinking sea water is harmful
core.p: Sea water has a much higher salt concentration than body fluids. If you drink it, water would leave your cells by osmosis into the salty fluid around them, and your kidneys would need to use even more water to get rid of the extra salt. You would become more dehydrated, not less.
bullets: Sea water has a **more concentrated** salt solution than blood plasma.
Cells lose water by **osmosis** into more concentrated solutions, so cells shrink and stop working properly.
The kidneys must excrete the excess salt in urine, which uses up water.
This is why survivors adrift at sea can die of thirst while surrounded by water.
So in dry countries, salt must be removed from sea water before it can be used.

core.p: Desalination means removing dissolved salts from sea water (or salty groundwater) to make potable water. It is used in countries where there is too little fresh water, for example in drought or in hot, dry regions with a coastline.
bullets: Used in areas with **low rainfall** or **drought**, where rivers, lakes and groundwater cannot supply enough water.
Examples include countries in the Middle East, parts of Australia and some islands.
Two main methods: **distillation (thermal)** and **reverse osmosis (membranes)**.
Both methods need a lot of **energy**, so desalinated water is **expensive**.
The salty waste (**brine**) must be disposed of, and returning it to the sea can harm marine organisms.

callouts.p: The removal of dissolved salts from sea water to produce potable water.

core.p: In distillation, sea water is heated until the water boils and evaporates. The salts do not evaporate, so they are left behind. The water vapour is then cooled in a condenser, where it condenses back into liquid water that has almost no salt. This copies the evaporation and condensation stages of the water cycle.
bullets: Step 1: **heat** sea water so water **evaporates** (boils).
Step 2: **salts are left behind** in the container.
Step 3: water vapour passes into a **condenser**, which is cooled (often by cold sea water).
Step 4: the vapour **condenses** into pure liquid water, which is collected.
Large amounts of **fuel or electricity** are needed to boil water, so it is costly and may release carbon dioxide if fossil fuels are burned.
Minerals may be added back afterwards so the water tastes normal.

fig.cap: Desalination by distillation. Heating makes water evaporate from sea water, leaving the salts behind in the flask. The vapour cools and condenses in the condenser and drips into the beaker as potable water.

core.p: In reverse osmosis, sea water is pushed at high pressure against a **partially permeable membrane**. Water molecules are forced through the membrane, but salt ions are too large to pass and are left behind. This is the reverse of normal osmosis, where water would move into the salty side.
bullets: Sea water is first **filtered** to remove solid particles and organisms.
High pressure is applied to the **salty side** of a partially permeable membrane.
Water is forced from the **more concentrated** solution to the **less concentrated** side, the opposite direction to osmosis.
**Salt ions cannot pass** through the membrane, so the water collected is low in salt.
Needs a lot of **energy** to create the high pressure, and membranes are expensive and need replacing.
Reverse osmosis usually uses less energy than distillation, so it is now the most common large-scale method.

head: Feature
Distillation
Reverse osmosis
rows: Membrane lets water through, not salt

callouts.p: In osmosis water moves from dilute to concentrated. Reverse osmosis uses pressure to force water from concentrated (sea water) to dilute (fresh water).

fig.cap: Reverse osmosis. A pump puts sea water under high pressure. Water molecules are forced through the partially permeable membrane but salt ions are held back, so potable water collects on the other side.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to weigh up desalination. It solves a real problem in dry countries, but it has costs for money, energy and the environment.
bullets: Advantage: provides a **reliable supply of potable water** where there is little rainfall.
Advantage: the sea is an almost **unlimited source** of water.
Disadvantage: needs **large amounts of energy**, so it is **expensive**.
Disadvantage: if the energy comes from **fossil fuels**, it releases carbon dioxide, adding to global warming.
Disadvantage: concentrated **brine** waste can harm sea life when returned to the sea.
Disadvantage: sea water intakes can trap and kill small marine organisms.
Using renewable energy (such as solar power in sunny desert countries) reduces some of these problems.

callouts.p: For an evaluate question, give at least one advantage, at least one disadvantage, then a conclusion, for example: worthwhile where there is no alternative, especially if solar power is used.

analogy.p: Think of the water cycle as a giant solar-powered still. The Sun is the heater that boils off fresh water from the salty sea, the cold upper air is the condenser, clouds are the storage tank and rain is the tap that delivers clean water onto the land. A distillation desalination plant is just a small human-built copy of the same thing, except we have to pay for the fuel. Where it breaks down: the real water cycle does not boil water; evaporation happens below 100 °C, and the 'tap' is not controlled, so some places get floods while others get drought.

terms.d: The continuous movement of water between oceans, atmosphere, land and organisms.
Liquid water changing into water vapour using heat energy, for example from the sea surface.
The loss of water vapour from plant leaves, mainly through the stomata.
Water vapour cooling and turning into liquid water droplets, forming clouds.
Water falling from clouds to the ground as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Water flowing over the land surface into streams, rivers and back to the sea.
Water that has soaked into soil and rock and is stored underground, for example in aquifers.
Water that is safe to drink.
Water containing no dissolved substances, only water molecules.
Removal of dissolved salts from sea water to produce potable water.
Boiling sea water and condensing the vapour, leaving salts behind.
Forcing water at high pressure through a partially permeable membrane that holds back salt ions.
A membrane that lets small molecules such as water through but not larger particles such as salt ions.
The very salty waste solution left over after desalination.
A long period with much less rainfall than normal, causing a shortage of fresh water.

mistakes.w: Transpiration is water evaporating from the sea.
mistakes.r: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves through the stomata.

mistakes.w: Condensation is when water turns into gas.
mistakes.r: Condensation is water vapour cooling and turning into liquid droplets.

mistakes.w: Potable water means pure water.
mistakes.r: Potable water is safe to drink; it can still contain small amounts of dissolved substances.

mistakes.w: Reverse osmosis is when water moves into the salty side by osmosis.
mistakes.r: High pressure forces water out of the salty solution through a partially permeable membrane, leaving salts behind.

mistakes.w: Desalination is cheap because sea water is free.
mistakes.r: Desalination needs large amounts of energy, so it is expensive.

mistakes.w: Distillation filters the salt out.
mistakes.r: In distillation water evaporates and the salts are left behind; the vapour is then condensed.

mistakes.w: Rain is salty because it comes from the sea.
mistakes.r: Salts are left behind when water evaporates, so precipitation is fresh water.

mistakes.w: The water cycle is driven by the wind.
mistakes.r: The water cycle is driven by heat energy from the Sun; wind only moves clouds and speeds up evaporation.

exam.q: Name the process by which water vapour is lost from the leaves of plants.
model: Transpiration
exam.tip: One word, spelled correctly. Do not write evaporation.

exam.q: What is meant by potable water?
model: Water that is safe to drink
exam.tip: Do not say pure water; that is a different idea.

exam.q: Describe how water in the sea becomes rain falling on land.
model: Heat from the Sun causes water to evaporate from the sea
Water vapour rises and cools
Water vapour condenses into droplets forming clouds
Clouds are blown over land and water falls as precipitation
exam.tip: Use the process names in the correct order: evaporation, condensation, precipitation.

exam.q: Explain why rain water is not salty even though much of it comes from the sea.
model: Only water evaporates from the sea
Salts are left behind in the sea
exam.tip: The key word is evaporation leaving salts behind.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the water cycle is important to living organisms.
model: Provides fresh water on land
For plants to photosynthesise / keep cells turgid
For animals to drink / replace water lost
exam.tip: Any two linked reasons; make each one about a use of water.

exam.q: Explain why some countries use desalination to produce drinking water.
model: Low rainfall / drought / hot dry climate
Not enough fresh water from rivers, lakes or groundwater
Have access to sea water
exam.tip: Link the lack of fresh water to the need for another source.

exam.q: Describe how distillation can be used to produce potable water from sea water.
model: Sea water is heated / boiled so water evaporates
Salts are left behind
Water vapour is cooled / condensed and collected
exam.tip: Three steps: evaporate, leave salt, condense.

exam.q: Describe how reverse osmosis produces potable water.
model: Sea water is filtered first
High pressure is applied to sea water
Water is forced through a partially permeable membrane
Salt ions cannot pass through the membrane
exam.tip: Must mention the partially permeable membrane and pressure.

exam.q: Suggest why reverse osmosis is used more than distillation in many modern desalination plants.
model: Reverse osmosis uses less energy than boiling water
So it is cheaper to run / produces less carbon dioxide
exam.tip: Compare energy, then link energy to cost or carbon dioxide.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of desalination to supply drinking water in a hot, dry coastal country.
model: Advantage: provides a reliable supply of potable water
Advantage: sea water is plentiful, so supply is not limited by rainfall
Disadvantage: requires large amounts of energy, so expensive
Disadvantage: burning fossil fuels for energy releases carbon dioxide / contributes to global warming
Disadvantage: brine waste can harm marine organisms
Conclusion: worthwhile if no other fresh water source, especially if solar power is used
exam.tip: Six-markers need both sides and a justified conclusion. Using the country's sunshine for solar power is a strong point.

exam.q: Explain why deforestation can reduce rainfall in an area.
model: Fewer trees so less transpiration
Less water vapour enters the atmosphere
Fewer clouds form by condensation so less precipitation
exam.tip: Follow the chain through each stage of the cycle.

worked.q: A student says 'Desalination is just the water cycle in a factory.' Explain how far this is true for distillation.
steps: In the water cycle, heat from the Sun evaporates water from the sea, leaving salts behind.
In distillation, a heater boils sea water so water evaporates and salts are left behind: the same idea.
In the water cycle, water vapour cools and condenses into clouds.
In distillation, a condenser cools the vapour so it condenses into liquid water: the same idea again.
Differences: distillation uses fuel or electricity rather than free solar energy, and produces concentrated brine waste.
worked.ans: Largely true: distillation copies evaporation and condensation, but it needs costly energy and makes brine waste.

worked.q: A desalination plant uses 3.5 kWh of energy to make 1 m³ of potable water by reverse osmosis. A town needs 20 000 m³ per day. How much energy is needed per day, and what does this suggest?
steps: Energy per day = energy per m³ × volume needed.
Energy = 3.5 kWh × 20 000 m³.
Energy = 70 000 kWh per day.
This is a very large amount of energy, so the water will be expensive.
If this energy comes from burning fossil fuels, lots of carbon dioxide is released.
worked.ans: 70 000 kWh per day; desalination is energy-hungry, so it is expensive and can add to carbon dioxide emissions unless renewable energy is used.

bio_edx.8.12.summary: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, but plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas directly; they need nitrogen in compounds such as **nitrates** to make **proteins** (and DNA). The **nitrogen cycle** uses several groups of bacteria to convert nitrogen between forms: **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** turn nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds, **decomposers** release ammonia from dead matter, **nitrifying bacteria** turn ammonia into nitrates, and **denitrifying bacteria** return nitrogen gas to the air. Farmers increase soil nitrates using **fertilisers** and **crop rotation** with legumes, which have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their **root nodules**.

core.p: Nitrogen is an essential element in **amino acids**, and so in **proteins**. It is also found in DNA. Every organism needs a supply of nitrogen to grow, because growth means making new cells, which need new proteins.
bullets: Air is about **78% nitrogen gas (N2)**, but N2 is very **unreactive**: the two atoms are held by a strong triple bond.
Plants and animals **cannot use nitrogen gas directly**.
Plants absorb nitrogen as **nitrate ions** from the soil through their **roots** by **active transport**.
Plants use nitrates (with glucose from photosynthesis) to make **amino acids**, then **proteins**.
Animals get nitrogen by **eating** plants or other animals and digesting their proteins.
Plants lacking nitrates show **stunted growth** and **yellow older leaves**.

callouts.p: There is lots of nitrogen in the air but it is in a form that plants and animals cannot use. Bacteria do most of the work of converting it.

core.p: The nitrogen cycle is the series of processes that move nitrogen between the air, the soil and living organisms. Most of the conversions are carried out by different types of bacteria, each doing one job.
bullets: **Nitrogen fixation**: nitrogen gas to ammonium compounds / nitrates (nitrogen-fixing bacteria, lightning).
**Feeding**: nitrogen passes along food chains as proteins.
**Decay (ammonification)**: decomposers turn proteins and urea in dead matter and waste into **ammonia**.
**Nitrification**: nitrifying bacteria turn ammonia into **nitrites** then **nitrates**.
**Denitrification**: denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates into **nitrogen gas**.
**Absorption**: plant roots take up nitrates.

fig.cap: The nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use. Plant protein passes to animals by feeding. Decomposers turn dead matter and waste into ammonium compounds, nitrifying bacteria convert these to nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.

core.p: Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of unreactive nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds such as ammonium ions or nitrates. Because N2 has such a strong triple bond, fixation needs a lot of energy.
bullets: **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** in the soil and in **root nodules** of legumes convert N2 into **ammonium compounds**.
**Lightning** provides enough energy to make nitrogen react with oxygen, forming nitrogen oxides that dissolve in rain and reach the soil as **nitrates**.
The **Haber process** in industry fixes nitrogen to make ammonia, which is used to make **artificial fertilisers**.
Without fixation, the amount of usable nitrogen in soils would steadily fall as denitrification returns it to the air.

callouts.p: The conversion of nitrogen gas from the atmosphere into nitrogen compounds (such as ammonium compounds or nitrates) that plants can use.

core.p: **Legumes** are plants such as peas, beans and clover. Their roots have small swellings called **root nodules** that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria. This is an example of **mutualism**: both partners benefit.
bullets: The bacteria fix nitrogen gas from the **air spaces in the soil** into **ammonium compounds**.
The plant uses these to make **amino acids and proteins**, so legumes grow well even in nitrate-poor soil.
In return, the plant supplies the bacteria with **sugars (carbohydrates)** made in photosynthesis, which the bacteria use for energy.
The nodules also give the bacteria a protected place to live.
When the legume dies, its protein-rich tissues are decayed, **adding nitrogen compounds to the soil** for the next crop.
Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria also exist in the soil, not just in nodules.

callouts.p: Bacteria give the plant ammonium compounds; the plant gives the bacteria sugars. Both benefit.

fig.cap: A legume such as a pea plant has root nodules. Inside each nodule are nitrogen-fixing bacteria that convert nitrogen gas from the soil air into ammonium compounds for the plant, in exchange for sugars.

core.h: Feeding and decay: putting nitrogen back in the soil
core.p: Nitrogen passes from plants to animals as protein when animals eat. Eventually all organisms die and animals produce waste. **Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) break down the proteins in dead bodies and the urea in urine and faeces, releasing the nitrogen as **ammonia**, which forms ammonium compounds in the soil.
bullets: Animals digest plant protein into **amino acids** and use them to build their own proteins.
Excess amino acids are broken down in the liver to make **urea**, which is excreted in **urine**.
Decomposers feed on **dead organisms, faeces and urine**.
They break down **proteins and urea** and release **ammonia / ammonium compounds** into the soil. This is called **decay** or **ammonification**.
Decomposers need warmth, moisture and oxygen to work quickly.

core.p: Plants cannot absorb ammonium compounds well, so they must be converted into nitrates. **Nitrifying bacteria** in the soil do this in two steps. They need **oxygen**, so nitrification happens in well-aerated soil.
bullets: Step 1: nitrifying bacteria convert **ammonia (ammonium compounds) into nitrites**.
Step 2: other nitrifying bacteria convert **nitrites into nitrates**.
Nitrifying bacteria are **aerobic**: they need oxygen.
Ploughing and good drainage keep soil aerated and help nitrification.
The nitrates produced are absorbed by plant roots by active transport.

callouts.p: Soil bacteria that convert ammonia (ammonium compounds) into nitrites and then into nitrates.

core.p: **Denitrifying bacteria** convert nitrates in the soil back into **nitrogen gas**, which returns to the atmosphere. This lowers soil fertility. Denitrifying bacteria thrive in **waterlogged, anaerobic** soils where there is little oxygen.
bullets: Denitrifying bacteria convert **nitrates into nitrogen gas**.
They are most active in **waterlogged soils** with **little oxygen** (anaerobic conditions).
This **reduces the nitrate content** of the soil, so plants grow less well.
Farmers reduce denitrification by **draining** fields and **ploughing** to let air in.
Denitrification completes the cycle by returning nitrogen to the air.

callouts.p: Nitrifying bacteria make nitrates (good for plants). Denitrifying bacteria destroy nitrates and release nitrogen gas (bad for farmers). Do not mix them up.

core.h: Why farmers need to add nitrogen
core.p: In a natural ecosystem, nitrogen taken up by plants is returned to the soil when they die and decay. On a farm, crops are **harvested and removed**, so the nitrogen in them never returns to that field. Over time the soil runs short of nitrates and yields fall.
bullets: Harvesting removes **proteins (nitrogen)** from the field.
Soil nitrate falls, so new crops grow poorly: **stunted growth, yellow leaves, lower yield**.
Farmers replace the nitrogen using **fertilisers** or **crop rotation**.
More nitrates means more **protein synthesis**, so more **growth** and higher **yields**.

core.p: Fertilisers add nitrogen compounds to the soil. They may be **artificial (inorganic)**, for example ammonium nitrate made using the Haber process, or **natural (organic)**, such as manure and compost. Organic fertilisers must be decomposed first, and their nitrogen is then converted to nitrates by nitrifying bacteria.
bullets: **Artificial fertilisers** contain nitrates or ammonium salts that plants can use **quickly**; the exact amount of nutrient is known.
**Manure and compost** release nitrogen **slowly** as they are decayed by decomposers and then nitrified.
Manure also improves **soil structure** and recycles waste.
Making artificial fertilisers by the Haber process uses **lots of energy**, often from fossil fuels.
**Too much fertiliser** or rain soon after application causes nitrates to **leach** (wash) out of soil into rivers and lakes.

head: Type
Example
Speed of nitrate release
Notes
rows: Known amounts; can leach easily; energy to make
Needs decomposers and nitrifying bacteria; improves soil

core.p: Nitrates are very soluble. If too much fertiliser is used, the excess washes into rivers and lakes and causes **eutrophication**, which can kill fish and other aquatic animals.
bullets: Nitrates **leach** into water and cause **rapid growth of algae** (an algal bloom).
Algae cover the surface and **block light**, so water plants below cannot photosynthesise and die.
**Decomposers (bacteria)** feed on the dead plants and algae and multiply.
Their **aerobic respiration** uses up the **oxygen** dissolved in the water.
Fish and other animals **die from lack of oxygen**.
Farmers can reduce this by using the correct amount of fertiliser and not spreading it before heavy rain.

callouts.t: The oxygen comes from bacteria, not algae
callouts.p: Marks are given for saying decomposers / bacteria use up the oxygen in respiration. Do not say the algae use up the oxygen.

core.p: Crop rotation means growing **different crops in a field in successive years**, in a set sequence. One year in the rotation is a **legume** crop, such as peas, beans or clover. Its root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria, so it adds nitrogen compounds to the soil instead of using them up.
bullets: Legumes **fix nitrogen** using bacteria in their **root nodules**, raising soil nitrogen.
After harvest, the remains of the legume (roots and sometimes the whole plant) are **ploughed into the soil**.
**Decomposers** break down the plant proteins into ammonia, and **nitrifying bacteria** convert it into **nitrates**.
The following crop (e.g. wheat) then has **more nitrates** for growth, so **less artificial fertiliser** is needed.
Different crops use different nutrients and suffer from different **pests and diseases**, so rotation also stops pests building up.
Cheaper than buying fertiliser and causes **less leaching**, but in the legume year the farmer may grow a less valuable crop.

callouts.p: Growing a sequence of different crops in the same field in successive years, including a nitrogen-fixing legume, to keep the soil fertile.

fig.cap: A three-year crop rotation. Wheat and potatoes use up nitrates. In year 3 a legume crop with nitrogen-fixing root nodules is grown and then ploughed in, so decomposers and nitrifying bacteria restore nitrates in the soil.

core.h: Comparing ways of keeping soil fertile
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare or evaluate methods. Use cost, speed, environmental effects and yield in your answer.
bullets: **Artificial fertiliser**: fast-acting and precise, high yields, but costly, energy-intensive to make and risks **eutrophication**.
**Manure**: cheap if the farmer keeps animals, recycles waste and improves soil, but releases nitrogen slowly and unpredictably and is bulky.
**Crop rotation**: cheap and sustainable, reduces fertiliser use and pests, but one year grows a lower-value crop.
Good drainage and ploughing reduce **denitrification** and help **nitrification**, keeping more nitrate in the soil.

callouts.p: For 'explain how crop rotation increases yield', follow the nitrogen: N2 fixed in nodules, plant protein, ploughed in, decomposers make ammonia, nitrifying bacteria make nitrates, next crop absorbs nitrates, makes more protein, grows more.

analogy.p: Imagine nitrogen gas as raw ore that no one can use. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are the refinery that turns ore into usable metal (ammonium compounds). Plants are factories that build products (proteins) from it, and animals buy those products. Decomposers are the scrap yard that breaks old products back into scrap (ammonia), nitrifying bacteria re-cast scrap into the standard parts plants can buy (nitrates), and denitrifying bacteria are leaks that let usable parts escape back as ore (nitrogen gas). Fertiliser is buying parts in bulk from outside. Where it breaks down: in a real factory someone plans each step, but in the soil each type of bacterium is simply getting energy for itself, and the conditions (oxygen, water) decide which bacteria win.

terms.d: The cycling of nitrogen between the atmosphere, soil and living organisms, mostly driven by bacteria.
Conversion of nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds such as ammonium compounds or nitrates.
Bacteria in soil or root nodules that convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds.
Swellings on the roots of legumes that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
A plant such as pea, bean or clover that has root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
A relationship between two species in which both benefit, e.g. legumes and nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter and waste, releasing ammonia from proteins and urea.
Aerobic soil bacteria that convert ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates.
Bacteria in waterlogged, anaerobic soil that convert nitrates into nitrogen gas.
Nitrogen-containing ions absorbed by plant roots and used to make amino acids and proteins.
Nitrogen compounds produced by decomposers and nitrogen-fixing bacteria; converted to nitrates by nitrification.
A substance added to soil to supply mineral ions such as nitrates; artificial or natural (manure).
Growing different crops in a field in successive years, including a legume, to maintain soil fertility.
Soluble ions such as nitrates being washed out of the soil by rain into rivers and lakes.
Excess nutrients in water causing algal growth, plant death, bacterial respiration, oxygen loss and death of aquatic animals.

mistakes.w: Plants absorb nitrogen gas from the air through their leaves.
mistakes.r: Plants absorb nitrates from the soil through their roots; they cannot use nitrogen gas.

mistakes.w: Nitrifying bacteria turn nitrates into nitrogen gas.
mistakes.r: Denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates into nitrogen gas; nitrifying bacteria turn ammonia into nitrites then nitrates.

mistakes.w: Legumes contain nitrogen in their nodules which they release.
mistakes.r: Root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria that convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds.

mistakes.w: Plants need nitrogen to make glucose / for energy.
mistakes.r: Plants need nitrates to make amino acids and proteins for growth.

mistakes.w: Crop rotation works because different crops need different amounts of water.
mistakes.r: A legume crop with nitrogen-fixing bacteria increases soil nitrogen; when ploughed in, decay and nitrification produce nitrates.

mistakes.w: In eutrophication the algae use up all the oxygen.
mistakes.r: Decomposing bacteria feeding on dead plants and algae use up the oxygen in respiration.

mistakes.w: Denitrifying bacteria work best in dry, aerated soil.
mistakes.r: Denitrifying bacteria thrive in waterlogged, anaerobic soil.

mistakes.w: Fertilisers give plants energy.
mistakes.r: Fertilisers supply mineral ions such as nitrates for making proteins; energy comes from light via photosynthesis.

exam.q: Name the type of bacteria that convert nitrates into nitrogen gas.
model: Denitrifying bacteria
exam.tip: Spell the prefix clearly: de-nitrifying.

exam.q: Explain why plants need nitrates.
model: To make amino acids
Which are made into proteins for growth
exam.tip: Proteins is the key word; mention growth for the link.

exam.q: Describe the role of nitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.
model: Convert ammonia / ammonium compounds into nitrites
Then convert nitrites into nitrates
exam.tip: Two steps: ammonia to nitrites, nitrites to nitrates.

exam.q: Explain how the relationship between a pea plant and the bacteria in its root nodules benefits both organisms.
model: Bacteria fix nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds
Plant uses these to make amino acids / proteins
Plant provides bacteria with sugars / carbohydrates from photosynthesis
Bacteria use sugars for respiration / energy; nodule gives shelter
exam.tip: Two marks for each partner. This is mutualism.

exam.q: Explain why waterlogged soils contain fewer nitrates.
model: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen / is anaerobic
Denitrifying bacteria thrive and convert nitrates to nitrogen gas
Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen so less nitrification occurs
exam.tip: Mention both types of bacteria for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why farmers need to add nitrogen to fields when this is not needed in a natural forest.
model: Crops are harvested and removed from the field
So the nitrogen in them is not returned by decay
In a forest, dead organisms decay in place and nitrogen is recycled
exam.tip: The key idea is removal of biomass by harvesting.

exam.q: Explain how crop rotation including a legume can increase the yield of a wheat crop grown the following year.
model: Legumes have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds / nitrogen compounds
Legume remains are ploughed into the soil
Decomposers break down proteins into ammonia
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates
Wheat absorbs more nitrates to make more protein so grows more / higher yield
exam.tip: Follow the nitrogen atom from air to wheat protein. Each step is a marking point.

exam.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using manure instead of artificial fertiliser.
model: Advantage: cheaper / recycles waste / improves soil structure / less leaching
Disadvantage: releases nitrates slowly / nutrient content unknown / bulky to spread
exam.tip: One clear point each; avoid vague words like better for the environment.

exam.q: Explain how adding too much nitrate fertiliser to a field can lead to the death of fish in a nearby lake.
model: Excess nitrates leach into the lake
Algae grow rapidly / algal bloom
Algae block light so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die
Decomposers / bacteria break down dead plants and multiply
Bacteria respire aerobically and use up dissolved oxygen
Fish die due to lack of oxygen
exam.tip: Classic six-mark chain. Say bacteria use up the oxygen.

exam.q: State two ways in which nitrogen gas can be fixed other than by bacteria.
model: Lightning
Haber process / industrial manufacture of fertiliser
exam.tip: Both are well-known extras to bacterial fixation.

exam.q: Explain why farmers plough and drain their fields to keep soil nitrate levels high.
model: Ploughing / draining adds oxygen to the soil
Aerobic nitrifying bacteria / decomposers work faster, producing more nitrates
Fewer anaerobic conditions so less denitrification
exam.tip: Link oxygen to which bacteria are favoured.

worked.q: A farmer measured wheat yields in two fields. Field A grew wheat every year and yielded 6.0 tonnes per hectare. Field B grew clover the previous year and yielded 7.5 tonnes per hectare with no extra fertiliser. Calculate the percentage increase and explain it.
steps: Percentage increase = (new - old) ÷ old × 100.
Clover is a legume with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules, which converted nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds.
When the clover was ploughed in, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria converted its protein nitrogen into nitrates.
The wheat absorbed more nitrates, made more protein and grew more.
worked.ans: 25% increase, because the clover crop raised soil nitrate levels via nitrogen fixation, decay and nitrification.

worked.q: Trace one nitrogen atom from the air into a cow's muscle and back to the air.
steps: Nitrogen gas in the air is fixed into an ammonium compound by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in a clover root nodule.
The clover uses it to make amino acids and protein.
A cow eats the clover and digests the protein into amino acids, which it absorbs and uses to build muscle protein.
When the cow dies, decomposers break down the muscle protein, releasing ammonia.
Nitrifying bacteria convert the ammonia to nitrites and then nitrates.
In waterlogged soil, denitrifying bacteria convert the nitrates into nitrogen gas, returning the atom to the air.
worked.ans: Air (N2) to fixation to plant protein to cow protein to ammonia (decay) to nitrates (nitrification) to N2 (denitrification).

bio_edx.8.13.summary: An **indicator species** is an organism whose presence, absence or abundance tells us about the level of pollution in an environment. In water, **sludge worms** and **bloodworms** (and rat-tailed maggots) indicate **polluted, low-oxygen** water, while **stonefly larvae** and **freshwater shrimps** indicate **clean, well-oxygenated** water. In air, **lichens** indicate air quality because many species are killed by **sulfur dioxide**. You must be able to **evaluate** using indicator species compared with direct chemical measurements.

core.p: Some organisms can only survive in a narrow range of conditions. If we know what conditions a species needs, finding it (or not finding it) in a place tells us about the conditions there. These organisms are called **indicator species**, and they are used as **evidence** of how polluted water or air is.
bullets: An indicator species is **sensitive** to a particular change, such as low oxygen or high sulfur dioxide.
**Presence** of a sensitive species suggests **low pollution**.
**Presence in large numbers** of a tolerant species, with sensitive species absent, suggests **high pollution**.
Indicator species show the **long-term** effect of pollution, because they live in the place over time.
Scientists usually look at the **whole community** of indicator species, not just one organism.

callouts.p: A species whose presence, absence or numbers can be used as evidence of the level of pollution in an environment.

core.p: Water pollution in rivers often comes from **raw sewage** or **fertiliser run-off**. These add organic matter or nutrients to the water, and the result is a fall in the **dissolved oxygen** concentration, which is why oxygen-sensitive animals are good indicators.
bullets: Sewage contains **organic matter** that **bacteria (decomposers)** feed on.
The bacteria multiply and their **aerobic respiration** uses up **dissolved oxygen**.
Fertiliser run-off causes **eutrophication**: algal blooms, plant death, more decomposers and loss of oxygen.
Animals that need **high oxygen levels** die or move away.
Animals adapted to **low oxygen** survive and, with less competition, their numbers increase.

callouts.p: Most water indicator species tell you about the dissolved oxygen concentration, which falls when water is polluted with sewage or fertiliser.

core.p: Some invertebrates can survive in water with very little oxygen. Finding large numbers of them, with no oxygen-sensitive species, indicates polluted water.
bullets: **Sludge worms (Tubifex)**: live in mud at the bottom; have haemoglobin and can survive very low oxygen levels.
**Bloodworms** (midge larvae): red because they contain **haemoglobin**, which lets them take up oxygen even when there is very little in the water.
**Rat-tailed maggots** (hoverfly larvae): have a long breathing tube like a snorkel that takes air from the surface, so they do not depend on dissolved oxygen.
These species can live in clean water too, but are **outcompeted** there; in polluted water they thrive in **large numbers**.
High numbers of these, plus a lack of clean-water species, means **high pollution / low oxygen**.

callouts.p: Bloodworms and sludge worms can live in clean water too. It is a high abundance of them together with the absence of sensitive species that indicates pollution.

core.p: Other invertebrates need **high concentrations of dissolved oxygen** and cannot survive pollution. Finding them shows the water is clean.
bullets: **Stonefly larvae**: very sensitive; need **high oxygen** levels; only found in clean, fast-flowing water.
**Freshwater shrimps**: need **well-oxygenated** water; found in clean to slightly polluted water.
**Mayfly larvae** are also often used as clean-water indicators.
Their presence means the water is **clean / unpolluted** with a **high dissolved oxygen** concentration.
Their disappearance is an early warning that pollution is happening.

head: Indicator
What it indicates
Why
rows: Haemoglobin lets it survive low oxygen
Breathing tube takes air from surface

core.h: A river downstream of a sewage outfall
core.p: A classic exam context is a river with a sewage outfall. Samples taken at different distances downstream show a clear pattern in oxygen and in the indicator species present.
bullets: **Upstream** of the outfall: high oxygen; stonefly larvae and freshwater shrimps present; many species.
**Just downstream**: bacteria decompose sewage and use up oxygen, so oxygen falls sharply; stoneflies disappear; sludge worms and bloodworms increase greatly.
**Further downstream**: sewage has been broken down, water is re-oxygenated by mixing with air and by photosynthesis, so oxygen recovers.
Clean-water species **return** and pollution-tolerant species decrease.
The **diversity** (number of different species) is lowest where pollution is worst.

callouts.p: Data questions: first describe the pattern using numbers from the graph, then explain it using oxygen and bacterial respiration.

fig.cap: Changes downstream of a sewage outfall. Oxygen falls where bacteria decompose the sewage, then recovers further downstream. Stonefly larvae disappear where oxygen is low, while sludge worms reach their peak, then the pattern reverses as the river recovers.

core.p: **Lichens** grow on tree bark, walls and rocks. A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga. Lichens absorb water and minerals directly from the air and rain over their whole surface, so they also absorb pollutants. Many lichens are very sensitive to **sulfur dioxide (SO2)**, which is released when fossil fuels containing sulfur are burned.
bullets: Sulfur dioxide comes from burning **fossil fuels** (e.g. coal in power stations, vehicles) and forms **acid rain**.
Lichens have **no roots or protective outer layer**, so they take in SO2 dissolved in rain directly.
Different lichen species have **different tolerances** to SO2.
**Crusty (crustose)** lichens are the most tolerant; **leafy (foliose)** lichens are fairly sensitive; **bushy (fruticose)** lichens are the most sensitive.
**Many lichen species, including bushy ones** = **clean air**.
**Few or no lichens, only crusty ones** = **high SO2 / polluted air**.
Black spot fungus on rose leaves is another SO2 indicator: it is absent where SO2 levels are high, because SO2 kills it.

callouts.p: The more lichen species growing in an area, the lower the level of sulfur dioxide in the air.

fig.cap: Number of lichen species on trees at increasing distances from a city centre. Near the centre sulfur dioxide is high and only tolerant crusty lichens survive. Further out, air is cleaner and leafy and then very sensitive bushy lichens appear.
