core.p: Replanting trees does not instantly restore biodiversity. Grade 9 answers evaluate how effective it is.
bullets: Trees take **many years** to grow, so habitats recover slowly
Plantations of a **single species** (monoculture, e.g. conifers) support far fewer species than the original mixed forest
Planting **native, mixed species** gives the greatest benefit for biodiversity
Ancient forest has complex soils and communities that cannot be quickly recreated
Land used for trees cannot be used for farming, which may conflict with food production and local livelihoods

core.p: Conservation often has to be balanced against human needs. Exam questions may ask you to evaluate a scheme.
bullets: Local people may rely on land for farming, fuel or hunting, so schemes work best with **community involvement** and alternative income such as ecotourism
Conservation is **expensive** (staff, monitoring, enforcing laws)
Protecting one species may affect others (e.g. protecting a predator reduces its prey)
Success can be measured by monitoring **population size** and **species diversity** over time, e.g. with quadrats or capture-recapture

callouts.p: Give a benefit, a drawback and a justified conclusion. Use data from the question if provided.

analogy.t: Biodiversity as a woven safety net
analogy.p: An ecosystem is like a safety net woven from many threads, where each thread is a species and the knots are feeding relationships. With many threads, cutting one barely matters because others take the load (stability). Conservation repairs and protects the threads, captive breeding is like re-spinning a nearly broken thread, wildlife corridors tie separate pieces of net together, and reforestation reweaves a large hole. The analogy breaks down because threads in a real ecosystem are alive and change over time, some species (keystone species) hold far more weight than others, and an extinct species can never be re-spun.

terms.d: The variety of living organisms in an area, including species, genetic and habitat diversity.
The variety of species in a particular habitat or area.
The variety of all species living on Earth.
When no individuals of a species remain alive anywhere.
A species at serious risk of becoming extinct.
Protection of species and habitats to maintain biodiversity.
Breeding endangered animals in zoos or sanctuaries to increase their numbers, often for later release.
Releasing animals of a species into an area where they used to live.
A strip of habitat linking separate habitat areas so animals can move between them.
Replanting trees in an area where forest has been cut down.
Large-scale removal of trees from forests.
The dependence of species on one another for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
The variety of alleles within a population of a species.
Tourism based on visiting natural habitats and wildlife, which can fund conservation.
A store of seeds kept in cold, dry conditions to preserve plant genetic diversity.
Growing a single species of plant over a large area.

mistakes.w: Biodiversity is the number of animals in an area.
mistakes.r: Biodiversity is the variety of species (all organisms) in an area, not the number of individuals.

mistakes.w: Reforestation produces oxygen so animals can breathe.
mistakes.r: Reforestation provides habitats and food and removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere by photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Captive breeding saves the species (no further detail).
mistakes.r: It increases population size, then individuals are released into the wild; breeding is planned to avoid inbreeding.

mistakes.w: Conservation is good because animals are nice to look at.
mistakes.r: Give scientific benefits: stable food webs, medicines, crop genes, ecosystem services, ecotourism income.

mistakes.w: Planting any trees restores biodiversity fully.
mistakes.r: Monoculture plantations support few species; mixed native trees are needed and recovery takes many years.

mistakes.w: Reforestation and afforestation mean the same.
mistakes.r: Reforestation replants where forest was removed; afforestation plants trees where there was no forest.

mistakes.w: High biodiversity stops any species dying out.
mistakes.r: High biodiversity makes the ecosystem more stable because predators have alternative food sources if one species declines.

mistakes.w: Zoos keep animals so that people can see them.
mistakes.r: For conservation, zoos run captive breeding, research and education programmes.

exam.q: State what is meant by biodiversity.
model: The variety of (different) species / organisms in an area
exam.tip: Use the word variety.

exam.q: Give two reasons why it is important to maintain biodiversity.
model: Ecosystem stability / interdependence of species
Source of medicines / food / genes for crops / ecotourism / moral reasons
exam.tip: Two different categories of benefit.

exam.q: Explain why an ecosystem with high biodiversity is more stable than one with low biodiversity.
model: More complex food web / more feeding relationships
If one species declines others can use alternative food sources
exam.tip: Link to interdependence.

exam.q: Give one way reforestation reduces climate change.
model: Trees absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis / store carbon in wood
exam.tip: CO2, not oxygen.

exam.q: Explain how reforestation can increase biodiversity.
model: Provides habitats / shelter for animals
Provides food sources for many species
More niches so more species can live there / especially if native mixed trees used
exam.tip: Habitats plus food plus variety of species.

exam.q: Explain how a captive breeding programme can help prevent the extinction of an endangered species.
model: Animals protected from predators / poaching / disease in zoo
Population size increases through breeding
Offspring released into the wild / protected habitats to increase wild numbers
exam.tip: Finish with release, not just breeding.

exam.q: Suggest why captive breeding programmes keep records of which animals are mated.
model: To avoid inbreeding
To maintain genetic diversity / reduce risk of genetic disorders
exam.tip: Genetic diversity helps survival of change.

exam.q: Explain how a wildlife corridor can help conserve a species.
model: Links separate / fragmented habitats
Animals can move to find food and mates, increasing genetic diversity
exam.tip: Mention mates and breeding.

exam.q: Suggest two reasons why replanting a rainforest may not restore its original biodiversity.
model: Trees take many years to grow / mature
Only one or a few species may be planted / some species already extinct / soil changed
exam.tip: Think time and variety.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of conservation and reforestation to maintain biodiversity.
model: Biodiversity gives stable ecosystems, medicines, food crops genes and ecotourism
Captive breeding increases numbers of endangered species and allows reintroduction
But captive-bred animals may lack survival skills; low genetic diversity; costly
Protected areas and laws protect whole habitats and reduce hunting
Reforestation restores habitats, absorbs CO2, reduces soil erosion and flooding
But trees take years to grow; monocultures support fewer species; conflict with farmland
Conclusion: most effective when methods combined and local people involved
exam.tip: Benefits, methods, limits and conclusion.

worked.q: Data example: 2 hectares of a forest reserve had 12 bird species before reforestation of the surrounding land and 30 species 15 years later. Calculate the percentage increase and explain it.
steps: Increase = 30 - 12 = 18 species
Percentage increase = 18 / 12 x 100 = 150%
Explain: replanted trees provide new habitats, nesting sites and food (insects, seeds, fruit)
More niches available so more species can live there
It took 15 years because trees take a long time to mature
worked.ans: 150% increase in bird species, due to new habitats and food from reforestation.

worked.q: Data example: A captive-bred population of oryx grew from 40 to 250. 60 were released. What percentage were released, and why release them into a protected area?
steps: Percentage released = 60 / 250 x 100 = 24%
A protected area has laws against hunting, so poaching is reduced
Habitat is maintained so released animals have food and space
Animals can breed in the wild, increasing genetic diversity of the wild population
worked.ans: 24% were released; protected areas remove the original threats so the released animals can survive and breed.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why scientists want to protect plant species in rainforests that have not yet been studied. (3 marks)
steps: Many medicines come from plants (e.g. aspirin from willow)
Undiscovered plants may contain chemicals that could be new drugs
They may also contain useful genes for crop breeding
If they become extinct this potential is lost forever
worked.ans: Undiscovered rainforest plants may provide new medicines or useful genes, which would be permanently lost if they became extinct.

bio_edx.8.8.summary: **Food security** means having enough safe, nutritious food to feed a population, now and in the future. For Edexcel (triple) you must describe the biological factors that threaten it: the **increasing human population**, **changing diets in wealthier populations** (more meat and dairy), **new pests and pathogens**, **environmental change** such as climate change, the **sustainability** of farming methods, and the **cost of agricultural inputs** such as fertiliser and pesticides. Grade 9 answers link each factor to a cause-and-effect chain, for example explaining that energy is lost between trophic levels, so feeding crops to animals feeds fewer people than eating the crops directly.

core.p: A population is **food secure** when everyone has reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food to stay healthy. **Food insecurity** is when people cannot be sure of getting enough food. Food security is threatened when demand for food rises faster than supply, or when supply falls.
bullets: Food security depends on both **supply** (how much food is produced) and **access** (whether people can obtain and afford it).
Supply depends on biological factors such as crop yield, pests, disease, soil quality, water and climate.
Demand depends on the size of the population and what people choose to eat.
A country can produce plenty of food overall yet still have food-insecure people if food is too expensive or unevenly shared.
The spec lists six factors: population, diets, pests and pathogens, environmental change, sustainability, cost of inputs.

callouts.p: Having enough food to feed a population: all people have access to enough safe, nutritious food at all times.
Learn the list: increasing population, changing diets, new pests and pathogens, environmental change, sustainability, cost of agricultural inputs.

core.p: The world population has risen from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion today and is projected to approach 10 billion by 2050. More people means more food is needed, but the amount of farmland, fresh water and fertile soil is limited.
bullets: More people means **greater demand** for food.
Land is also needed for **housing, roads and industry**, so farmland can be lost as populations grow.
Clearing forests to create more farmland (**deforestation**) reduces biodiversity and can damage soils.
Growing populations need more **fresh water**, and agriculture already uses most of the fresh water humans take.
The fastest population growth is often in countries that are already food insecure, so the problem is concentrated there.

callouts.p: Population growth increases demand. If food production cannot increase at the same rate, food security falls.

core.h: Factor 2: changing diets in wealthier populations
core.p: As people become wealthier they tend to eat **more meat and dairy** and more varied, imported foods. This matters because of energy transfer between trophic levels: only around 10% of the energy in one trophic level is passed to the next.
bullets: Livestock use most of the energy in their food for **respiration, movement and keeping warm**, and some is lost in faeces and urine.
So feeding crops to animals and then eating the animals gives **far less food energy** than eating the crops directly.
More meat in diets means more land and more crops are needed to grow **animal feed** (for example soya and cereals).
Demand for exotic foods means land in poorer countries may be used to grow **cash crops for export** instead of food for local people.
Rich countries can outbid poorer countries for food on world markets, raising prices.

head: Diet
Trophic level eaten
Effect on food security
rows: Fewer people fed per hectare, more land and water used

callouts.p: Energy is lost at each trophic level (mostly through respiration and as heat), so a longer food chain means less energy reaches humans.
Do not just say meat is expensive. The biological reason is energy loss between trophic levels.

core.p: **Pests** (such as insects that eat crops) and **pathogens** (disease-causing microorganisms such as fungi, bacteria and viruses) reduce crop yields and kill livestock. New ones are a particular threat because crops have no resistance and there may be no treatment yet.
bullets: Global trade and travel move pests and pathogens to **new areas** where they have **no natural predators** or competitors, so their populations grow rapidly.
Many crops are grown as **monocultures** of genetically similar plants, so a pathogen that can infect one plant can spread through the whole field.
Pests and pathogens **evolve** by natural selection: random mutations can produce **resistance to pesticides** or the ability to infect previously resistant crop varieties.
Example: new strains of **wheat stem rust** fungus have destroyed wheat crops in Africa and Asia.
Historic example: **potato blight** (a pathogen) destroyed potato crops in Ireland in the 1840s, causing famine.
Warmer climates can let pests survive winters and spread to new regions.

callouts.p: Overuse of a pesticide kills non-resistant pests, leaving resistant ones to survive, reproduce and pass on the resistance allele, so the pesticide stops working.

fig.cap: Why a newly arrived pest or pathogen can sharply reduce yields: with no predators and no crop resistance, its population grows rapidly and spreads through genetically similar crops.

core.p: Crops need suitable temperatures, enough water and fertile soil. **Environmental change**, especially **climate change** caused by rising greenhouse gas levels, alters these conditions and can reduce yields.
bullets: Changing **rainfall patterns** cause **droughts** in some areas, so plants lack water for photosynthesis and wilt.
Other areas get **floods**, which waterlog soils, wash away crops and remove fertile topsoil.
Higher temperatures can push crops beyond their **optimum temperature**, reducing yield; extreme heat can denature enzymes.
**Desertification** and **soil erosion** turn farmland into land that cannot grow crops.
Rising sea levels can flood low-lying farmland with salt water.
Warmer conditions can help pests and pathogens spread to new areas.
Some places may gain longer growing seasons, but overall many of the world's poorest regions are expected to lose out.

callouts.p: Explain WHY: less water or a temperature above the optimum reduces the rate of photosynthesis, so less glucose is made and growth and yield fall.

core.p: **Sustainable** food production meets today's needs without reducing the ability of future generations to produce food. Many methods that increase yield in the short term damage the resources farming depends on.
bullets: **Overfishing** removes fish faster than populations can reproduce, so stocks collapse and the food source is lost.
Intensive farming can **deplete soil nutrients** and organic matter, and can cause soil erosion.
Overuse of fertilisers can wash into rivers, causing **eutrophication** that harms aquatic food sources.
Taking too much water for **irrigation** lowers water tables and dries up rivers and lakes.
Land used to grow crops for **biofuels** is land not used to grow food, which can raise food prices.
Sustainable approaches include fishing quotas and net mesh sizes, crop rotation, using manure or compost, and reducing food waste.

callouts.p: Meeting the needs of people today without damaging the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

core.p: **Agricultural inputs** are everything a farmer has to buy to grow food: fertilisers, pesticides, seeds, animal feed, fuel, machinery and water for irrigation. High costs reduce how much food farmers can produce and raise the price of food.
bullets: **Fertilisers** supply nitrates, phosphates and potassium for plant growth; without them yields fall.
Manufacturing nitrogen fertiliser uses a lot of energy from fossil fuels, so its price rises when energy prices rise.
**Pesticides** and herbicides are needed to protect yields but are expensive.
Fuel for tractors, transport and refrigeration adds cost at every stage.
Farmers in poorer countries may be unable to afford inputs, so their yields stay low.
Higher input costs are passed on as **higher food prices**, so poorer people can afford less food.

callouts.p: Even if food exists, people are food insecure if they cannot afford it.

core.p: In exam answers, the best marks come from linking factors together rather than listing them. Most factors either raise demand or lower supply, and several make each other worse.
bullets: Population growth plus richer diets means demand for food rises even faster than population.
Climate change helps pests spread and makes droughts more likely, both lowering yield.
Unsustainable farming damages soil, so more fertiliser is needed, increasing input costs.
Higher fuel costs raise both fertiliser prices and transport costs.
Biofuel crops compete with food crops for land, linking sustainability, cost and supply.

head: Factor
Increases demand or reduces supply?
rows: Increases demand for crops and land

core.p: Although the spec point focuses on the threats, questions often ask how food security could be improved. Each solution should tackle a named factor.
bullets: Breeding or **genetically modifying** crops to be resistant to pests, disease or drought.
**Biological control** of pests (using a natural predator) reduces pesticide use and costs.
Eating less meat so more crops feed people directly.
Reducing food waste at every stage of the food chain.
Sustainable fishing with **quotas** and larger net mesh sizes so young fish can breed.
Using **crop rotation** and nitrogen-fixing plants to reduce fertiliser costs.

callouts.p: Always state which factor your solution addresses and how, for example: drought-resistant crops reduce the effect of environmental change on yield.

core.p: Edexcel often gives graphs or tables, such as population against food production or yield against rainfall, and asks you to describe, explain or evaluate.
bullets: Describe the trend first, quoting numbers with units from the graph.
Then explain the trend using a biological factor (for example, less rainfall means less water for photosynthesis).
Calculate changes or percentage changes if asked: percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100.
Point out limitations: correlation does not prove causation, data may come from only one region or a short time period.
Consider both sides when asked to evaluate, then give a justified conclusion.

callouts.p: Describe means say what the data shows; explain means give the biological reason. Do not mix them up.

analogy.p: Imagine a school canteen with a fixed number of tables (farmland) and one kitchen. More students arriving is population growth. Some students now want burgers instead of sandwiches, and each burger uses ten times the ingredients (changing diets and trophic-level energy loss). Mice getting into the store cupboard are pests. A broken freezer or a heatwave spoiling food is environmental change. Using up all the ingredients today so nothing is left for next week is unsustainable practice, and rising prices for ingredients is the cost of inputs. The analogy breaks down because a canteen can simply buy more food from outside, whereas the whole world has no outside supplier, and real crops and pests are living things that grow, reproduce and evolve.

terms.d: Having enough food to feed a population: all people have access to enough safe, nutritious food at all times.
When people do not have reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food.
An organism, often an insect, that damages crops or livestock and reduces yield.
A microorganism (bacterium, virus, fungus or protist) that causes disease.
The amount of crop or food produced per unit area of land.
Growing a single crop variety over a large area, so plants are genetically similar.
The position of an organism in a food chain, such as producer or primary consumer.
The percentage of energy in one trophic level that is passed to the next, typically around 10%.
Meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
Resources farmers must buy, such as fertilisers, pesticides, seeds, feed, fuel and machinery.
A substance added to soil to provide mineral ions such as nitrates, phosphates and potassium for plant growth.
An inherited ability of a pest to survive a pesticide, which spreads through the population by natural selection.
Long-term change in global temperatures and weather patterns, mainly caused by increased greenhouse gases.
The process by which fertile land becomes desert, often due to drought, overgrazing or deforestation.
Removing fish faster than the population can replace itself by reproduction.
A fuel made from plant material, whose crops can compete with food crops for land.

mistakes.w: Food security means a country has lots of food.
mistakes.r: Food security means all people have access to enough safe, nutritious food at all times; access and affordability matter, not just total amount.

mistakes.w: Eating meat is bad for food security because meat is expensive.
mistakes.r: Energy is lost between trophic levels (around 90%, mainly through respiration and heat), so more crops and land are needed to produce meat than to feed people directly.

mistakes.w: Pests become resistant because they get used to the pesticide.
mistakes.r: A random mutation gives some pests resistance; they survive, reproduce and pass on the allele by natural selection.

mistakes.w: Climate change makes it hotter so crops grow faster.
mistakes.r: Temperatures above the optimum, droughts and floods reduce photosynthesis and yield; overall many regions lose yield.

mistakes.w: New pests are dangerous because they are bigger or stronger.
mistakes.r: New pests may have no natural predators and crops have no resistance to them, so their populations grow rapidly.

mistakes.w: Using more fertiliser always improves food security.
mistakes.r: Fertiliser is costly and overuse can cause eutrophication and is unsustainable; benefits must be weighed against costs.

mistakes.w: A growing population needs more food so we should just clear more forest.
mistakes.r: Clearing forest reduces biodiversity and can cause soil erosion, so it is not sustainable and can lower future yields.

mistakes.w: Listing the factors without explaining them.
mistakes.r: Each factor must be linked to its effect on food supply or demand, for example: new pathogen, lower yield, less food available.

exam.q: What is meant by the term food security?
model: Having enough food to feed a population / everyone has access to enough safe, nutritious food.
exam.tip: Learn the definition word for word.

exam.q: Give two biological factors that can reduce food security.
model: Any two from: increasing human population; changing diets / more meat eaten; new pests or pathogens; environmental change / climate change; unsustainable farming; cost of agricultural inputs.
exam.tip: Use the spec wording for easy marks.

exam.q: Explain why an increasing human population threatens food security.
model: More people means greater demand for food.
Land and resources such as water are limited / farmland lost to housing, so supply may not keep up.
exam.tip: Give a demand idea and a supply limit.

exam.q: Explain why a shift to diets high in meat in wealthier countries reduces global food security.
model: Energy is lost at each trophic level.
Through respiration / heat / movement / waste by livestock.
So less energy reaches humans from meat than from eating crops directly.
More land / crops needed to grow animal feed, so fewer people can be fed.
exam.tip: Always mention energy loss between trophic levels; it is the key biological idea.

exam.q: A new fungal pathogen of wheat has spread from Africa to Asia. Explain how this could affect food security.
model: Wheat plants have no resistance to the new pathogen.
Pathogen spreads quickly / wheat grown as monoculture / no natural control.
Crop yield falls so less food is available / food prices rise.
exam.tip: Follow the chain: cause, spread, yield, food.

exam.q: Explain how a pest population can become resistant to a pesticide.
model: Random mutation gives some pests resistance.
Pesticide kills non-resistant pests; resistant ones survive and reproduce.
Resistance allele passed to offspring, so proportion of resistant pests increases.
exam.tip: Never say pests adapt or get used to it.

exam.q: Suggest how climate change could reduce crop yields.
model: Droughts mean less water for photosynthesis / floods destroy crops or erode soil.
Temperatures above the optimum for growth / pests spread to new areas.
exam.tip: Link to photosynthesis or pests for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why the cost of agricultural inputs affects food security.
model: Farmers who cannot afford fertilisers / pesticides get lower yields.
Higher costs raise food prices so poorer people cannot afford enough food.
exam.tip: Name a specific input.

exam.q: Give one reason why overfishing is not sustainable.
model: Fish are removed faster than they can reproduce, so stocks fall / collapse.
exam.tip: Use the word reproduce.

exam.q: Discuss the biological factors that affect the level of food security in the world.
model: Increasing population raises demand for food while land and water are limited.
Wealthier populations eat more meat; energy lost between trophic levels so more crops and land needed.
New pests and pathogens reduce yields; crops have no resistance and pests may evolve pesticide resistance.
Environmental change such as drought, floods and high temperatures reduces photosynthesis and yield.
Unsustainable practices such as overfishing or soil degradation reduce future food supply.
Cost of inputs such as fertiliser and pesticides limits production and raises food prices.
exam.tip: Cover a range of factors, each with a linked explanation; a list alone will not reach the top band.

exam.q: Suggest two ways scientists could reduce the effect of new pathogens on food security.
model: Breed or genetically modify crops to be resistant to the pathogen.
Use biological control / fungicides / crop rotation / quarantine checks on imported plants.
exam.tip: State how each method reduces losses.

worked.q: 100 000 kJ of energy in a field of grain is fed to cattle. The energy transfer efficiency from grain to cattle is 10%. A person needs about 10 000 kJ per day. How many person-days of food are provided if (a) people eat the grain directly (assume all energy available) or (b) people eat the cattle?
steps: (a) Energy available directly = 100 000 kJ.
Person-days = 100 000 / 10 000 = 10 person-days.
(b) Energy in cattle = 10% of 100 000 = 0.10 x 100 000 = 10 000 kJ.
Person-days = 10 000 / 10 000 = 1 person-day.
Comparison: eating the grain directly feeds 10 times as many person-days.
worked.ans: (a) 10 person-days; (b) 1 person-day. Feeding crops to livestock reduces the number of people fed tenfold because about 90% of energy is lost between trophic levels.

worked.q: Model 4-mark answer: explain how climate change and new pests could together reduce food security in a country that relies on maize.
steps: Climate change may cause drought, so maize has less water for photosynthesis and grows less.
Warmer temperatures allow a pest to survive the winter and spread into the country.
The pest has no natural predators there and maize has no resistance, so the pest population increases rapidly through the monoculture.
Both effects lower maize yield, so less food is produced and prices rise, so fewer people can afford enough food.
worked.ans: Drought reduces photosynthesis and yield; warmer climate lets pests spread with no predators or resistance; lower yields and higher prices reduce food security.

worked.q: World food production rose from 2.0 to 2.6 billion tonnes, while population rose from 6.0 to 7.8 billion. Calculate the percentage increase in each and comment on food security.
steps: Both rose by the same percentage, so food per person stayed the same.
But diets with more meat mean more crop is used as animal feed, and food is not evenly shared, so some people remain food insecure.
worked.ans: Both increased by 30%; food per person is unchanged, but uneven access and changing diets mean food security is not guaranteed.

bio_edx.8.9.summary: The Earth has a fixed amount of each chemical element, so the materials living things are made of, such as **carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, water and mineral ions**, must be **recycled** between the **abiotic** (non-living) and **biotic** (living) parts of an ecosystem. Producers take materials in from the air, soil and water; feeding passes them along food chains; and **respiration, excretion, combustion and decomposition** return them to the abiotic environment to be used again. Unlike energy, which flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat, matter goes round in cycles, and **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) are essential to keep those cycles turning.

core.p: Living organisms are built from a small number of elements, mainly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, plus mineral ions such as phosphate and magnesium. The Earth is effectively a closed system for matter: no new atoms arrive, so the same atoms must be used again and again.
bullets: There is a **finite** (limited) amount of each element on Earth.
If materials were not recycled, they would stay **locked up in dead bodies and waste**, and new organisms could not grow.
Recycling returns materials to the **abiotic** environment (air, soil, water) so **producers** can take them up again.
The atoms in your body have previously been part of other organisms, rocks, the air and the oceans.
The cycles named in the Edexcel spec are the **carbon cycle**, **water cycle** and **nitrogen cycle**.

callouts.p: Matter is recycled; energy is not. Energy enters as light and leaves as heat, but atoms go round and round.

core.p: An ecosystem is made of the living community plus the non-living environment. Materials move between these two parts and within the living part.
bullets: **Biotic components**: producers (plants, algae), consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi).
**Abiotic components**: the atmosphere, soil, rocks, oceans, rivers and lakes.
Materials in the abiotic part are in simple inorganic forms such as **carbon dioxide, water and nitrate ions**.
In the biotic part they are built into complex **organic molecules** such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and DNA.
Cycling therefore means converting simple inorganic molecules into complex organic ones and back again.

core.p: Materials enter living things almost entirely through **producers**. Plants and algae take in simple inorganic substances and use energy from light to build them into organic molecules.
bullets: **Photosynthesis** takes in **carbon dioxide** from the air (or dissolved in water) and **water** from the soil and makes **glucose**: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen.
Roots absorb **water** by osmosis and **mineral ions** such as nitrate, phosphate and magnesium by **active transport**.
Plants use glucose plus **nitrate ions** to make **amino acids and proteins**.
Magnesium ions are needed to make **chlorophyll**; phosphate is needed for DNA and cell membranes.
Without producers, no new materials could enter food chains.

callouts.p: Write photosynthesis for carbon entering plants and absorption or active transport for mineral ions; vague words like taken in lose marks.

core.p: Once materials are in producers, they pass to other organisms through **feeding**. Consumers digest the large organic molecules and use the products to build their own tissues.
bullets: Herbivores eat plants; carnivores eat other animals: materials move along **food chains and food webs**.
Digestion breaks large molecules (starch, proteins, lipids) into small soluble ones that are absorbed and reassembled into the consumer's own molecules.
Not all material eaten becomes new tissue: some is used in **respiration**, some is lost in **faeces** and **urine**.
When any organism dies, or sheds leaves, hair and skin, its materials become **dead organic matter** for decomposers.
Materials are therefore always moving: from producer to consumer to decomposer.

core.h: Step 3: from biotic back to abiotic
core.p: Several processes return materials to the air, soil and water, closing the cycle so that producers can use them again.
bullets: **Respiration** by all organisms releases **carbon dioxide and water** into the atmosphere.
**Excretion** returns waste such as **urea** (nitrogen) and water to the soil and water.
**Decomposition** of dead organisms and waste by microorganisms releases **CO2** and **mineral ions** such as ammonium and nitrate.
**Transpiration** releases water vapour from leaves into the air.
**Combustion** of wood and fossil fuels releases stored carbon as CO2.
Some material is stored for very long periods, for example carbon in fossil fuels or limestone.

core.p: **Decomposers** are mainly **bacteria and fungi**. They feed on dead organic matter and waste, breaking it down and releasing the materials it contains back into the environment. They are the key link that returns materials to the abiotic part of the ecosystem.
bullets: Decomposers secrete **enzymes** onto dead material; this is **extracellular digestion** (digestion outside their cells).
The enzymes break large insoluble molecules into **small soluble molecules**, which the decomposers absorb.
Decomposers use some of these molecules in **respiration**, releasing **carbon dioxide** to the air.
Other products, such as **mineral ions** (ammonium, nitrate, phosphate), are released into the soil, where plant roots can absorb them.
**Detritivores** such as earthworms and woodlice break dead matter into smaller pieces, increasing the **surface area** for decomposers to act on.
Without decomposers, dead material would pile up and nutrients would be locked away, so plant growth would stop.

callouts.p: A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead organic matter and waste, releasing materials back into the environment.
Decomposers release carbon dioxide by respiration. They do not photosynthesise and they do not release CO2 by digesting.

core.p: A key grade 9 idea is the difference between how matter and energy move through ecosystems. Matter is recycled indefinitely; energy enters as light, is passed along food chains in chemical form, and is eventually lost as **heat** to the surroundings.
bullets: Energy enters ecosystems as **light** captured by producers in photosynthesis.
At each trophic level, much energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat by **respiration**, so less is available to the next level.
Heat cannot be captured by producers, so energy **cannot be recycled**; ecosystems need a constant input of sunlight.
The atoms that carried that energy (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen) are not lost: they return to the air and soil as CO2, water and ions.
So an ecosystem is open for energy but (almost) closed for matter.

Energy

core.h: Example: carbon moving through an ecosystem
core.p: Following one carbon atom shows how biotic and abiotic components link together. (Full details are in 9.13.)
bullets: A carbon atom in **CO2 in the air** (abiotic) is taken in by a leaf during **photosynthesis** and becomes part of **glucose** (biotic).
The glucose may be turned into **starch, cellulose or protein** in the plant.
A rabbit **eats** the plant; the carbon becomes part of the rabbit's tissues.
The rabbit **respires**, releasing some carbon as CO2 back to the air.
When the rabbit dies, **decomposers** digest it and respire, releasing the rest of the carbon as CO2.
The carbon atom is back in the abiotic environment, ready to be used again.

core.p: Water and nitrogen also move between abiotic and biotic components. (Full details are in 9.14 and 9.15.)
bullets: **Water**: absorbed by roots, used in photosynthesis, lost by **transpiration**; drunk by animals and returned by respiration, sweating and urine; evaporation and precipitation move it through the abiotic part.
**Nitrogen**: most organisms cannot use **N2 gas** directly; **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** convert it into compounds plants can use.
Plants absorb **nitrate ions** to make proteins; animals get nitrogen by eating plants.
Decomposers convert proteins and urea in dead matter and waste into **ammonium**, which bacteria convert to nitrates.
**Denitrifying bacteria** return nitrogen to the air as N2.

callouts.p: In every cycle, microorganisms do the job of returning materials to the abiotic environment. Mention them in any cycling answer.

core.h: Conditions that affect the rate of cycling
core.p: Because decomposition is carried out by living microorganisms using enzymes, anything that affects their growth and enzyme activity affects how quickly materials are recycled.
bullets: **Temperature**: warm conditions increase enzyme activity and decay rate; very high temperatures denature enzymes; cold slows decay.
**Water**: decomposers need moisture; dry conditions slow decay.
**Oxygen**: most decomposers respire aerobically, so decay is faster with oxygen; waterlogged soils slow decay.
**Number of decomposers and detritivores** and the **surface area** of the material.
Example: in tropical rainforests, decay is fast and nutrients recycle quickly; in cold, waterlogged peat bogs, decay is very slow and material builds up.

callouts.p: When decay is slow or prevented, materials are locked away for a long time, which is how peat, coal, oil and gas formed.

core.p: Humans change how fast materials move between stores, which can unbalance cycles.
bullets: Burning **fossil fuels** releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years, increasing CO2 in the air.
**Deforestation** reduces photosynthesis, so less CO2 is removed from the air.
Harvesting crops removes minerals from fields, so farmers add **fertilisers** to replace them.
Excess fertiliser running into rivers can cause **eutrophication**.
Composting returns nutrients from waste to the soil, supporting cycling.

core.p: Exam questions often give a diagram of a cycle with missing labels, or ask you to describe how a material moves from one place to another.
bullets: Name the **process** at each step (photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition, excretion, combustion).
Say whether each store is **biotic or abiotic** if asked.
State the **form** the material is in (CO2, glucose, protein, nitrate ions).
Include **decomposers** and say they **respire** to release CO2 and release mineral ions.
For explain questions, link each step with because or so.

callouts.p: On cycle diagrams, check arrow direction: photosynthesis points from air to plants; respiration points from organisms to air.

analogy.p: Think of Earth's elements as a library of LEGO bricks with no shop to buy more. Producers check bricks out of the library (air, soil, water) and build models (organic molecules). Consumers take models apart and rebuild them into their own designs. When models are broken or abandoned, decomposers are the librarians who dismantle them and put the bricks back on the shelves so they can be borrowed again. Energy is like the battery power used to snap bricks together: once used it is gone as heat and must be supplied fresh by the Sun. The analogy breaks down because real atoms are not reused in exactly the same shape: they are chemically rearranged into new molecules, and some bricks can be locked away for millions of years in fossil fuels or rocks.

terms.d: All the organisms living in an area together with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
A living part of an ecosystem, such as producers, consumers and decomposers.
A non-living part of an ecosystem, such as air, water, soil and rocks.
The continuous movement of a substance or element between biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem.
An organism, such as a plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets its food by eating other organisms.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead organic matter and waste, releasing materials to the environment.
An animal such as an earthworm that feeds on dead material, breaking it into smaller pieces.
Digestion outside cells, where enzymes are secreted onto food and soluble products are absorbed.
The process in which producers use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
An exothermic process in all living cells that releases energy from glucose, producing carbon dioxide and water in aerobic respiration.
Removal of waste products of metabolism, such as urea and carbon dioxide, from the body.
Inorganic ions, such as nitrate, phosphate and magnesium, absorbed by plant roots from the soil.
A carbon-containing molecule made by living things, such as glucose, protein or lipid.
Burning of fuels in oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water.

mistakes.w: Energy is recycled in ecosystems.
mistakes.r: Energy flows through ecosystems and is lost as heat; only materials (matter) are recycled.

mistakes.w: Decomposers eat dead things and turn them into soil.
mistakes.r: Decomposers secrete enzymes to digest dead matter, absorb the products and release CO2 by respiration and mineral ions into the soil.

mistakes.w: Plants get their food from the soil.
mistakes.r: Plants make glucose by photosynthesis from CO2 and water; they absorb mineral ions (not food) from the soil.

mistakes.w: Plants take in nitrogen gas from the air.
mistakes.r: Plants absorb nitrogen as nitrate ions from the soil; N2 gas must first be fixed by bacteria.

mistakes.w: Decomposers release CO2 by photosynthesis or by breaking food down.
mistakes.r: Decomposers release CO2 by respiration.

mistakes.w: Materials are recycled because they are used up.
mistakes.r: Materials are recycled because the amount on Earth is finite; atoms are not destroyed, just moved between stores.

mistakes.w: Animals put carbon back into the air only when they die.
mistakes.r: Animals return carbon continuously by respiration (and excretion); decomposition of their bodies returns the rest after death.

mistakes.w: Using vague words such as plants take in carbon.
mistakes.r: Name the substance and process: plants absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

exam.q: Give one example of an abiotic component of an ecosystem.
model: Any one: air / atmosphere / water / soil / rock.
exam.tip: Abiotic means non-living.

exam.q: Explain why materials need to be cycled in an ecosystem.
model: There is a finite / limited amount of each material on Earth.
So materials must be returned to the environment to be used again by producers / new organisms.
exam.tip: Use the word finite or limited.

exam.q: Name the process by which carbon moves from the atmosphere into producers.
model: Photosynthesis.
exam.tip: One word, spelled correctly.

exam.q: Describe the role of decomposers in the cycling of materials.
model: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi.
They secrete enzymes to break down dead organisms / waste.
They respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
They release mineral ions (e.g. nitrates) into the soil, which plants absorb.
exam.tip: Include enzymes, respiration and mineral ions.

exam.q: State two processes that return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
model: Any two: respiration; combustion; decomposition (respiration by decomposers).
exam.tip: Decomposition counts because decomposers respire.

exam.q: Describe how nitrogen moves from the soil into an animal.
model: Plant roots absorb nitrate ions from the soil.
Plants use nitrates to make proteins / amino acids.
The animal eats the plant and digests the protein, using the amino acids to make its own proteins.
exam.tip: Follow the material through each organism.

exam.q: Explain the difference between how energy and materials move through an ecosystem.
model: Materials are recycled / move in cycles between biotic and abiotic components.
Energy flows in one direction / enters as light.
Energy is lost to surroundings as heat (by respiration) and cannot be reused.
exam.tip: Say heat cannot be used by producers.

exam.q: Explain why dead leaves decompose faster in a warm, moist forest than on a cold, dry mountain.
model: Warm temperature increases enzyme activity / rate of reactions of decomposers.
Moisture allows decomposers to grow / reproduce / enzymes to work.
Cold and dry conditions slow microbial growth and enzyme activity, so decay is slower.
exam.tip: Link conditions to enzymes and microorganism growth.

exam.q: Suggest why earthworms increase the rate at which nutrients are recycled.
model: Earthworms break dead matter into smaller pieces.
This increases the surface area for decomposers / enzymes to act on.
exam.tip: Surface area is the key phrase.

exam.q: Describe how materials are cycled through the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem. Use carbon as an example.
model: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (abiotic) is absorbed by producers for photosynthesis.
Carbon becomes part of glucose and other organic molecules in plants (biotic).
Carbon passes to consumers through feeding / food chains.
All organisms respire, releasing CO2 back to the atmosphere.
When organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) digest the remains using enzymes.
Decomposers respire, returning CO2 to the air; combustion of fuels also releases CO2.
exam.tip: Name the process and the biotic/abiotic store at each step to reach the top band.

worked.q: A diagram shows a cycle with stores: air, grass, sheep, dead matter. Label each arrow with a process and state whether each store is biotic or abiotic.
steps: Air to grass: photosynthesis (air is abiotic, grass is biotic).
Grass to sheep: feeding / eating (both biotic).
Grass and sheep to air: respiration.
Grass and sheep to dead matter: death, excretion (faeces, urine).
Dead matter to air: decomposition, as decomposers respire and release CO2.
Dead matter is organic but no longer living; it is broken down by biotic decomposers.
worked.ans: Photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, death/excretion, decomposition. Air is abiotic; grass and sheep are biotic.

worked.q: Model 4-mark answer: explain what would happen to the plants in a field if all the decomposers in the soil were killed.
steps: Dead leaves, roots and animal waste would not be broken down, so they would build up.
Mineral ions such as nitrates and phosphates in the dead matter would not be released into the soil.
Plants would not be able to absorb enough mineral ions, so they could not make enough proteins or chlorophyll.
Plant growth would slow and plants would show deficiency symptoms; less CO2 would also be released back to the air by decomposer respiration.
worked.ans: Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked in dead matter, mineral ions in the soil run out, and plant growth falls.

worked.q: In a woodland, leaf litter falls at 400 g per m2 per year. Decomposers break down 80% of it each year. How much leaf litter remains undecomposed per m2 per year, and what does this suggest?
steps: Amount decomposed = 0.80 x 400 = 320 g per m2.
Amount remaining = 400 - 320 = 80 g per m2 per year.
So each year 80 g per m2 builds up as litter or humus.
This shows most material is recycled quickly, but some is stored in the soil for longer.
worked.ans: 80 g per m2 per year remains; most nutrients are recycled each year, with a small amount stored as soil organic matter.
